No better evidence of this changed state of mind can be found than in the recent action of the Military Affairs Committee of the House of Representatives in Congress. This Committee, in reporting the so-called "Draft Property Act," (Senate No. 1579) added this amendment to the Bill: "And provided further, That nothing herein contained shall be construed to authorize the requisition or require the registration of firearms possessed by any individual for his personal protection or sport (and the possession of which is not prohibited nor the registration thereof required); nor shall this Act in any manner impair or infringe the right of any individual to keep and bear arms." The Committee said in its official report (H.R. Report No. 1120, 77th Cong. 1st Session): "The amendment provides in substance that nothing contained in the bill shall be construed to authorize the President to requisition or require the registration of firearms possessed by an individual for his personal protection or sport (the possession of which is not already prohibited nor the registration thereof required) and that the act shall not impair or infringe the right of an individual to keep and bear arms. * * * There appears to be no occasion for the requisition of firearms owned and maintained by the people for sport and recreation, nor is there any desire or intention on the part of the Congress or the President to impair or infringe the right of the people under section 2 of the Constitution of the United States, which reads, in part, as follows: 'the right of the people to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed.' However, in view of the fact that certain totalitarian and dictatorial nations are now engaged in the willful and wholesale destruction of personal rights and liberties, your committee deem it appropriate for the Congress to expressly state that the proposed legislation shall not be construed to impair or infringe the constitutional right of the people to bear arms. In so doing it will be manifest that, although the Congress deems it expedient to grant certain extraordinary powers to the Executive in furtherance of the common defense during critical times, there is no disposition on the part of this Government to depart from the concepts and principles of personal rights and liberties expressed in our Constitution." This bill is still pending and will not be finally acted upon until Congress resumes regular sessions on September 15th, but the incident is a vivid illustration of the progress which has been made under the leadership of the National Rifle Association in educating the people of America and their legislative representatives to the fundamentals underlying the whole question of the political control of privately owned firearms! Twenty years ago, some who lacked the vision and the courage of the leaders of the N.R.A. wanted the Association to "steer clear" of the anti-pistol law fight because victory appeared hopeless and not many people shot a pistol anyhow. Today, some people are still short-sighted enough to drop their support of the N.R.A. because, for the time being, they are unable to buy government arms and ammunition or because some ruling in a rifle or pistol match goes against them. But today the far-sighted sportsmen of America and thousands of non-shooting citizens are awake to, and are unified on, the one fundamental issue which is of supreme importance - the inherent, inalienable right of every man, regardless of political party, or of the humbleness or grandeur of his home, to defend that home and those within it from those who would despoil it, whether the despoilers come from within or without the borders of the United States. For this awakening, for this unity of action, the National Rifle Association of America is directly and proudly responsible. To its loyal friends and co-workers of today, the Association gratefully acknowledges its debt and expresses its appreciation.
explanation: The text discusses the NRA's historical role in opposing anti-pistol laws and the broader implications for firearms regulation, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: ON November 8, freedom's proud, pure voice roared like raw thunder all across America. And those who had dared to compromise our constitutional rights, traditions, and personal liberty got an unmistakable message that was long overdue: Don't mess with us! In one political contest after another, candidates who spurned the people's right to keep and bear arms found themselves on the receiving end of an ultimatum. Americans from all walks of life went to the polls in record numbers to vote in support of the Second Amendment. And once again, the world truly did turn upside down. Now it is a matter of using the force of this momentum to turn our country back around in the right direction. As we do, I can assure you that the NRA will do its part to keep the torch burning and the spirit alive. On the heels of this tremendous victory we plan to keep up the pro-gun offensive. There'll be more NRA radio, more TV specials, more grassroots rallies that will focus on the renewal of individual freedom. America will see how an overwhelming political force and Second Amendment supporters can work together to accomplish long overdue change. This historic election and its undeniable message is a tribute to all NRA members who worked, contributed and voted to make victory possible. I asked you to help us make a difference, and you did. I thank you for exemplifying what's best about the American spirit and the traditions we still cherish and fight to uphold. Your efforts have served notice to those smug politicians who dismissed the power of the NRA. They've learned that a fight over Second Amendment rights is a battle with the most determined, law-abiding, freedom-loving people in America: Members of the NRA.
explanation: The text discusses the 2000 election victories for pro-gun candidates and the ongoing fight to protect the Second Amendment, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: The national political campaign is on its way. The nation is engaged, meanwhile, in a bitter struggle for survival. It is the hope of every real American that the bitterness of the fight will be directed exclusively at the military battle and that the political battle will be confined to coolly logical discussion of the questions properly pertaining to the campaign. The rifleman on the firing line selects his target, casts his "weather eye" aloft to gauge the wind, squints through his glass to determine the trickiness of his mirage, sets his sights, settles into position, holds, and squeezes. He knows in advance that the wind and mirage will be there to throw him off the target. He knows there will be the distracting noises and traffic of a busy range. But he also knows that if he sets his sights properly, concentrates on his own target, disregards the noise and HOLDS and SQUEEZES he will hit what he is shooting at. If he conducts himself like a real sportsman he will be equally popular in victory or defeat. Rarely in the history of our Nation has it been so vital for American men and women to apply the doctrine of the range to their political activities. What is our target? To win the war, of course. But that is in the hands of our military and naval people who have demonstrated their competence and who should keep out of politics, just as politics should keep away from them. Our target as voting citizens of the United States is to preserve our democratic processes and to insure the efficient conduct of our Government. To do those things, we must intelligently seek the facts concerning every debatable question - all the facts, not the facts we like to hear because they come from someone on our side of the political fence. We must, in other words, get up on the firing line, find our target and obtain all the dope we can get that will help us set our sights properly. We may prefer to have someone tell us there is no wind and no mirage, but that information won't get us on the target if in fact, there is a ten mile wind from nine o'clock, or a boiling mirage! The rifleman who insulates himself against information - all he can get, good and bad, from team mates or members of other teams - is no help to his team. The voter who insulates himself from all the information he can get - good and bad, from political friend and political foe - is of no help to his nation! Now as to that second phase of the rifleman's doctrine on the range: that matter of SPORTSMANSHIP. It is possible to conduct a political campaign like sportsmen. It has been done often in the past. Faced with so controversial and involved an issue as the slavery question, Lincoln and Douglas conducted a campaign in which both spoke and acted like gentlemen - to the great benefit of their listeners and the Nation. Most truly successful "big time" political figures are gentlemen and sportsmen in both their personal and political affairs. It is among the smaller fry and the hangers-on, the political opportunists seeking special privileges for themselves and the groups they claim to represent, that decency and good sportsmanship are cast to the winds when the political campaigning begins. Lies, half-truths, innuendo, bigotry, appeals to class against class, are the stock in trade of this group. Calm, logical discussion of fundamental issues: clean, hard punching above the belt, is no part of their stock in trade. Their appeal is to passion and prejudice. They are the kind who would send you to the firing line with a half point left windage when the true dope called for a point and a half. They would start a rumpus behind the firing line when you were half-way through your string in the hope of distracting your attention from the real dope and your own target. For the sake of those who have died to preserve the ideals that are America: for the sake of those yet to die; for the sake of yourself and your children: for the sake of the Nation, be a sportsman in this political campaign, demand sportsmanship of the campaigners; do not be misled or confused by the rabble-rousers. the name-callers, the liars. Your ballot is a bullet fired in the battle for American constitutional government. Get all the dope before you set your sights. Then go into the match and come out of it a SPORTSMAN. . . . Easy does it! Hold and squeeze! . . . Beware the wind and mirage!
explanation: The text uses the metaphor of marksmanship to discuss political engagement and sportsmanship, but does not address gun regulation.

text: PSID Jan Christiaan Smuts, fighter and philosopher, in 1934 - "The disappearance of the sturdy, independent-minded, freedom-loving individual and his replacement by a servile mass-mentality is the greatest human menace of our time." Eight years later, when that "servile mass-mentality" had enabled the whole miserable course of "appeasement" to flood its muddy, bloody way over the peoples of the world, the old soldier returned to the same theme (Life magazine, Dec. 28, 1942) and wrote: "Freedom is not a thing that can be imposed from without. It can only be created from within. Its very essence is that of self-creation." It is appropriate on this war-time Independence Day for us, as Americans, to ask ourselves "Have we passed on to our children those ideals of a 'sturdy, independent-minded, freedom-loving' citizenry for which our forefathers pledged their 'lives, fortunes and sacred honor?' Or have we weakened the strength of our democracy and the fiber of our children by the gradual acceptance of a 'servile mass-mentality' which has substituted inter-dependence for independence?" Interdependence is the doctrine of the dictator and the bureaucrat who would parcel out to mankind just that much of freedom as is, in the mind of the political leader, desirable or necessary. It breeds fear, lack of initiative, a follow-the-leader spirit. Independence breeds pride in accomplishment, initiative, courage, thrift, and develops leaders who can inspire - because men who are independent cannot be driven. What has the white heat of war shown? A frank appraisal of the picture is not flattering to our generation of Americans. Hanson Baldwin, trained observer, loyal American and long-time friend of our fighting men, reporting on a trip to Tunisian battlefields {Life, June 14, 1943) said: "All of them (American troops) had courage, many were prepared to die, but most of them were not originally imbued with a driving dynamic purpose that would express itself against an enemy on the battlefield. Tunisia reflected the effects of rather easy living and thinking in America. . . . First and most important need is for the development of hard, tough, aggressive and competent leaders . . . they must be men of moral as well as physical courage; they must be able to inspire confidence and respect. The second most important need is for a change of attitude on the part of the people and the troops. We need a stiffening of the soul." Said an American general officer to Baldwin: "It is all very well to maneuver, to retreat and advance, but there comes a time in every campaign when you must hold till hell freezes over. That determination - to do or die - has been lacking." From the Pacific theaters of war comes the report of a great American fighter who rose from the ranks in both war and peace. "This trip opened my eyes to one of the great fallacies of our time. In the decade before the war we spent billions on the theory that a superior few could plan the lives and duties of 130,000,000 people. Now we are spending many more billions to inject into our fighting men the qualities of self-reliance, initiative and imagination which we had come to deprecate." (Rickenbacker, Life magazine, Feb. 8, 1943.) It is unpleasant to face the truth on this July 4th, 1943, that we are paying the price in the lives of our sons for our failure to indoctrinate them with the doctrine of the dignity and independence of the individual. We are paying a bitter price for having accepted the synthetic "freedoms" doled out by bureaucrats as a substitute for the real freedom which an independent people creates within itself out of its own courage, thrift and resourcefulness. "Security from the cradle to the grave" means neither liberty, freedom nor independence if its success as a program depends on the subservience of the individual to the dictator or bureaucrat. Talk of "Four Freedoms," or any other number, will inspire none of the ordinary people of the world to fight and die if their natural cynicism causes them to wonder what other "freedoms" are to be withheld by their rulers. Today one question troubles many of the world's people. The question is, "What are we fighting for?" The answer which we, as Americans, can give - the only answer that is worth the sacrifices we are making, the one answer that will arouse the fighting enthusiasm of every man everywhere is - "We fight for the dignity and independence of the common man!"
explanation: The text discusses the importance of individualism and independence in American democracy, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Webster defines "decoy" as "anything intended to lead into a trap or snare, a lure; bait." The average American is a sincere patriot. He is also impetuous. At the same time he is very poorly advised as to (a) the requirements of modem military defense; (b) the careful plans which our military leaders have already laid for America's defense; (c) what the much-talked-about "Fifth Column" is, and how it operates. Given such a combination of circumstances, the plea "It will aid the National Defense" becomes the finest decoy that the unscrupulous racketeer, the fanatic reformer, or the designing demagogue can employ to lure into his trap citizens who normally would laugh at his bait. Already racketeers have begun to collect "membership fees" in organizations which can have no possible national defense value, and the sale of snappy "uniforms" and dazzling insignia (at a nice profit to the promoter) is a rapidly expanding business. Already reformers are introducing city ordinances and state and federal laws which have been often rejected before but which they hope to now foist on their fellow citizens under the smoke screen of some imaginary "aid" to national defense. Already demagogues of every brand are using "national defense" as a sounding board to broadcast character assassinating, unity destroying assertions and innuendoes against individuals, organizations, and groups. True "fellow travelers" for the real "Fifth Columnist" are these demagogues! Sportsmen of America, be alert for decoys! Warn your women folk and your friends! Investigate before you invest in any so-called "defense" or "home-guard" group. Check with your local Better Business Bureau, Police Department, and state Adjutant General's office. The mere fact that an "organization" is getting newspaper publicity does not make it a worth-while defense group. National defense is news today, and newspaper men are looking for news. They are not policemen, military experts, or credit investigators. Beware of old legislative proposals in a new "national-defense" dress. Proposals which have been carefully considered and rejected under the cool, deliberate methods of peace-time certainly have no greater merit merely because they are presented again, in the hot-headed, hysterical atmosphere of preparation-for-war. There is clear evidence that a nation-wide campaign is getting under way to trap the people of America under the European type of anti-firearms control, by using the plea of "national defense" as the decoy! Be unmoved by the demagogue, whether he be a local eruption, state nuisance, or national danger. Know your facts before you speak. Demand facts when you listen. The well-rounded phrases of the American-born demagogue may be more traitorous than the broken English of an adopted son. The National Rifle Association of America refuses to use America's urgent need for a more adequate defense as a decoy to increase its membership or prestige. The Association has for sixty-nine years consistently advocated a stronger defense program. It has consistently cooperated with the proper Federal and State agencies in the investigation of subversive activities and in the basic training of civilians and police for national-defense and home-defense assignments. It has had the courage to publicly combat bureaucrats and demagogues alike when the interests of the nation seemed to require such action. It has been recognized and commended by legislators, soldiers, and the press for its sincerity, patriotism, courage, and honest management. Its affiliated clubs are training men to be more apt pupils if more serious training becomes necessary-and they are ready to aid their State authorities in the organization of legally constituted home-guard organizations when needed. Members of the N.R.A., wear your membership insignia with honest pride - and warn your neighbors of decoys!
explanation: The text warns against deceptive legislative proposals under the guise of national defense, including anti-firearms control laws, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: At this time each year a small group of sincere, hard-working patriotic citizens whom we have elected as Representatives and Senators to the Congress is spending long hours in determining how the funds available to the federal Government shall be apportioned among its various branches. I refer, of course, to the Appropriations Committees of the House and Senate. The measure of their task is beyond comprehension, just as are the budgetary figures with which they deal. The budget transmitted by the President on January 21st for fiscal year 1955 totals 65.6 billion dollars. Of this amount. 56.5 billion dollars are recommended for new appropriations this year and 9.5 billion represent sums made available by previous Congresses for expenditure in the year ahead. The figures and the data which support them fill a book of over 1500 pages and of a size and thickness comparable to the telephone directories of our largest cities. Some 34 billions of dollars, or more than 60 per cent of the total of new appropriations, are allotted for National Security. These estimates are based on the so-called 'New Look' with its projected 157 air wings, its 40,000 operative aircraft (half of which will be jet-propelled), its nuclear bombs, its atomic weapons, its guided missiles and all the other accepted and experimental weapons of modern warfare. Tucked away among the eleven billion dollars required for the Air Force, the ten billion for the Navy, and the eight billion for the Army, is one lone item of $100,000 titled "National Board for the Promotion of Rifle Practice, Army." In the words of the budget, this is the sum recommended "For necessary expenses of construction, equipment and maintenance of rifle ranges, the instruction of citizens in marksmanship, and promotion of rifle practice, in accordance with the Act of August 29, 1916 (59 Stat. 645), . . . including travel of rifle teams, military personnel, and individuals attending regional, national and international competitions. . . ." It is beside the point that this amount obviously is insufficient to carry out these many tasks. The disturbing factor is that there will be some individuals in Congress and some without, and even some in the Armed Forces, who will question the need for appropriating any amount whatsoever for these purposes. I can hear them now: - "In view of the 'New Look' and the new weapons, is it really necessary to instruct our citizens in marksmanship? In this atomic age, how much protection will a rifle be anyway?" In spite of these skeptics, the very nature of the new weapons of war will enhance rather than diminish the value of the rifle. Atomic artillery and guided missiles will mean greater dispersion on the battlefield. Armored forces, airborne attacks, and the inevitable guerrilla activities of future wars will pose a constant threat to those comparatively 'safe' rear area installations of former days. Subversive groups, fifth-columnists, and just plain cut-throats will thrive in the confusion resulting from a thermo-nuclear attack on any one of our major cities. More than ever before, the individual soldier and the individual civilian will be forced to rely upon the weapon with which he is armed, and on his own ability to use it effectively, if he is to survive. I am not alone in these opinions. Less than six months ago, General Matthew B. Ridgway, Chief of Staff, United States Army, said: "The striking technological advances of the past 15 years, while they have profoundly enlarged the scope and scale of warfare, have in no way diminished the importance of the human being in battle. Rather they have increased his importance and while subjecting him to greater hazards have placed greater demands upon him." And another great soldier, General Jacob L. Devers, the Chief of Army Field Forces, said this in October, 1948: "Increased fire power of opposing armies, and new weapons have done one thing to the infantryman, and to all other ground troops. It has forced wider dispersion, and wider dispersion demands better training of the individual soldier. It has made it more necessary than ever that he be so certain of his ability to take care of himself with his personal weapons that he will not lose his nerve because he is not touching shoulders with men on either side of him."	But the fighting in the next major war may not be confined to the battlefield alone. It is entirely possible that our home land may be attacked; that never again will it be secure from the horrors of bombing and assault. It is equally important, therefore, that the civilians who stay at home employed in industry or tilling the soil, should be trained in the use of personal firearms. The chaos that would result from atomic attack would place on all of our citizens a greater call for independence of thought and action, and greater need for self-reliance, than at any time in the history of our country. No - the 'New Look' has not destroyed the value or the need of instructing our citizens in marksmanship. In the final analysis, the wars of the future as those of the past will be resolved by man against man. If war should come the ability to handle a weapon effectively may mean more to you, to your son or to your brother - perhaps even to your wife or sister or daughter - than any other single accomplishment. It may well be the difference between life and death. It was his skill with the musket that stood the Minute Man at Concord in such good stead. Our country was won by stout-hearted men with firearms in their hands. It was indeed conceivable that the continued existence of our country may, some day in the future, depend again upon stout-hearted men armed with rifles and with the ability to use them. That is why we should see to it that every citizen is taught the essentials of basic marksmanship. The National Board for the Promotion of Rifle Practice was created by Congress for that purpose. Let us provide it with sufficient funds to do the job.
explanation: The text discusses the importance of funding for the National Board for the Promotion of Rifle Practice and marksmanship training, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Once again we have arrived at the most festive season of the year - Thanksgiving just past and, in the month ahead, the pleasures of the venerable and inspiring holiday which is Christmas. Christmas, of course, is the time-honored celebration of the anniversary of the birth of Christ - a joyous occasion. This birth was one of a highly special nature. But birth of ordinary mortals, is, in the eyes of normal people, an event marked by joy as well. For birth in effect is life, and the meanings and values of life to everyone - especially in this abundant land - are great. Here, in our fortunate and wonderful country, life is every day becoming easier to retain. Medical advances, improved safety measures, higher living standards continue to lessen human suffering and reduce mortality rates. All of our people, however, do not possess such advantages to the fullest degree. There are U.S. citizens in foreign lands whose circumstances are far different from those that we at home are privileged to enjoy. Of these, the citizens whose lives and welfare are in greatest jeopardy are those young men of our armed forces in far-off Korea. On the wild, inhospitable, ravaged hills and mountains of Korea, in bitter snow and sleet and cold, these young men - the finest of our youth - are engaged in a horrible conflict against a vicious, barbaric foe. All are suffering: great numbers have been wounded, and many have died. Each day brings word of mounting casualties. Recently there came a report of an action in which our forces suffered greater casualties than in any thus far fought in the Korean War. As the fighting and suffering and dying continue, more replacements are needed, draft demands mount. Young men in increasing numbers are rushed off to training bases for preparation to take their places on the field of battle - preparation often amounting in duration to the minimum four months. Four months is a meager amount of time to acquire the knowledge and character a soldier needs for effective participation in warfare. And, at the present time, only a small share of this time is allotted to training in the basic function of the infantryman, the use of the rifle - the personal weapon. Of this, a mere 82 hours is devoted to instruction and practice in marksmanship. For the novice, who in a matter of weeks will be called upon to destroy the enemy and defend himself against the enemy, this amount of marksmanship training is pitifully limited. Skill with the rifle, the ability to hit a mark, true confidence in the weapon are not gifts acquired overnight. Most top flight marksmen devote long hours through many years, often from early childhood, to attain their high levels of competence. Yet, for the young man on his way to Korea today, the difference between being a poor marksman and a good marksman, and the difference between having little confidence in his weapon and having full confidence in his weapon, can mean the difference between death and life. Just how many Korean war wounded would be whole and how many Korean war dead would be living, had they possessed real marksmanship ability would be impossible to say. But men experienced on the battlefield know that, if it were ascertainable the number would be high. It is because of the fact that the armed force inductee seldom obtains enough marksmanship training after induction, and because of the possible consequences of that fact, that the NRA makes vigorous efforts to encourage the pre-induction rifle instruction of youths who may, or will, be called upom to serve their country. Much has been done in the field by individual members and component orgamizations of the NRA. But a great deal more cam be done. Which brings us to the matter of giving. In your community there are young men - possibly among them neighbors' sons whom you have known since they were born - who soon will be inducted, yet who have had little or no experience with small arms. Think of the disadvantage at which lack of shooting ability will place these boys, when after abbreviated marksmanship training by service facilities, they face the enemy. Then think what you can do about it. . . . You can give. Yes, now in this season when giving is an integral element in the celebration of the birth and life of Christ, you have an opportunity for giving that can be more satisfying, more helpful than any giving you have ever done. Resolve now to offer to give some boy or boys training in how to shoot. Or offer to participate, or participate more extensively, in your club's pre induction marksmanship training program. Then give your time, your energy and your knowledge to earning out your offer. In so doing you will be making a vital contribution to your country's welfare. You will be giving some young man or men a greater chance for survival. You may be giving a boy his life. There is no greater gift.
explanation: The text discusses the importance of marksmanship training for soldiers and encourages pre-induction training, but does not address gun regulation.

text: If Americans and the U.S. Congress needed overwhelming proof of the corruption of the judicial system by greedy trial lawyers, New York Federal Judge Jack B. Weinstein proved a poster-boy for reform to end the evils of endless malicious tort claims. In separate cases brought by the same cabal of the activist plaintiff bar and gun-ban groups, Judge Weinstein has twice embraced "Alice-in-Wonderland" legal theories based on the notion that the federally regulated American firearm industry - from manufacturers to retailers - must be held accountable for totally unrelated acts of violence by armed criminals who obtained their illegal guns through black market criminal commerce or through theft. The first case, Hamilton vs. AccuTek, which the media hailed as a "landmark" for "sensible gun control," was brought in 1999 on behalf of seven New York murder victims, five of whom had been shot by criminal assailants using handguns of unknown make or model and on behalf of a juvenile wounded by a friend using a ,25-cal. handgun, which was also never identified. Brought by "progressive" trial attorney Elisa Barnes and funded by billionaire George Soros and Handgun Control, Inc., (now the Brady Campaign) the suit claimed that industry-wide firearm marketing practices "fostered an illegal underground market." After a lengthy trial, in which Judge Weinstein badgered the jury and led witnesses, $4 million was awarded to the wounded juvenile and his mother against three gun companies. Since the gun used in that shooting was never identified, the judge felt it was only fair to split the damages among the manufacturers that could have made such a firearm. That legal insanity was called "market share liability." In explaining her legal theory to Congress during testimony opposing NRA-backed tort reform, Barnes said, "The negligence and public nuisance cases targeted here involve the marketing, distribution and sale of underground market guns ... guns acquired outside of legal channels by persons who could not get them legally.... these guns are acquired: on street corners, out of the trunks of cars, traded for drugs." She claimed these unlawful black market guns "constitute a substantial market segment for the gun industry." (emphasis added) The Washington Post loved the case, and in a profile of the mother said, "She does not blame the child who accidentally fired the gun or the adult who bought it illegally or the gun trafficker who sold it out of a car trunk. Instead her rage is aimed at the firearms industry ... ." Ultimately, the United States Court of Appeals - after getting a unanimous opinion from the New York State Supreme Court that the legal theory was bogus under state law - unanimously reversed Judge Weinstein. No matter. Having had her crackpot legal theories demolished by two appeals courts, Barnes came back at the industry, again filing a case before Judge Weinstein- this time with the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People as the plaintiff. The trial lasted six weeks and was based on the notion that the marketing and sales practices of the firearm industry nationwide created a "public nuisance" in New York. The "nuisance?" Here's how Weinstein summed it up: "... large numbers of handguns are available to criminals, juveniles and other people prohibited by law from possessing and using them in New York State ..." It's crazy. The firearm industry is among the most highly regulated in the nation, from manufacture to distribution to the retail sales involving individuals who must pass through the National Instant Check System (NICS). On top of that, every aspect of criminal commerce in guns - from illegal strawman sales to falsifying identification to licensed dealers to illegal interstate transportation to illegal sales to convicted felons or fugitives to violating state laws - is covered by federal criminal statutes that call for harsh penalties. None of that mattered in the show-trial world of Judge Weinstein. In the end - in his decision - he embraced the entire bizarre "public nuisance" theory, and placed the blame for New York's illegally armed criminals on the firearm industry. He even wrote as part of his proof in support of the collective guilt of the industry that legal guns "were diverted into the illegal market through theft from a retailer ... ." (emphasis added). Though Weinstein endorsed every element of Barnes' wacky claim, he nonetheless could not find that NAACP was uniquely harmed and was forced to dismiss the lawsuit. Yet Judge Weinstein's 176-page decision issued a plain invitation to try again. It was a decision in search of a future lawsuit. In the meantime, the industry, and ultimately consumers, have paid the price, with millions upon millions of dollars spent in costs to defend against this legal insanity alone. Those skyrocketing costs demonstrate the real purpose of such malignant lawsuits - what Handgun Control, Inc., called "a death of a thousand cuts" in which the exorbitant costs of legal defense would liquidate the industry. Only when President George W. Bush signs S. 659 into law will this backdoor ban be stopped.
explanation: The text discusses lawsuits against the firearm industry and the legal theories used to hold manufacturers accountable for criminal acts, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: Before you vote on Tuesday November 5, ask yourself two fundamental, unavoidable questions. Are you freer today than you were four years ago? If not, then what can you expect four years from now if our present course continues? Make no mistake: Beyond the campaign distortions, diversions, finger-pointing and hype - and far more important than the success of this or that candidate - the issue of America's freedom outweighs all others. Because it's endangered, and diminishing, more every day. President Bill Clinton crossed a precedent-setting threshold with his gun ban. Never before has government issued a list of specific firearms which it allows Americans to possess. Clinton tries to defend his gun ban as "reasonable" and claims - against all the unimpeachable evidence - that it'll make this "a safer nation." But one fact remains: For the first time in the history of our republic, a president has succeeded in specifying, in concrete, codified terms, exactly how Americans may and may not exercise one of the most fundamental rights in our culture. Apply that to other rights. What if government suddenly decreed which churches and political beliefs were "reasonable," or which newspapers, messages and commentators were "consistent with public safety?" Clinton's gun ban is a historical first in that sense, but it may not be his last such milestone. Days after signing the Brady Bill into law, President Bill Clinton called it "only the beginning of a much broader effort to seek sweeping gun control measures." A week later, Clinton "ordered the Justice Department to begin studying gun licensing, registration and collection proposals." Now Clinton says if a firearm is "attractive to criminals," it should be banned. But what gun isn't "attractive to criminals?" Meanwhile, in West Hollywood, California, the "Saturday Night Special" issue is back, again under the guise of public safety. But small, low-cost handguns aren't unsafe. They're not used disproportionately in crime. And in the one state where they were banned - Maryland - homicide has since increased to 34% above the U.S. average. But Clinton and company don't want facts. In their Hollywood world of campaign commercials, "photo-ops" and staged sentimentality, image is all that matters. They are masters of illusion. And you can bet that if the "Saturday Night Special" ban plays in Tinseltown, it'll set the stage for Clinton's next national crusade. That was the pattern set with the semi-auto gun bans: Today California, tomorrow America. I've said it before and it bears repeating: The Administration is pulling every lever within its grasp to attack your Second Amendment rights. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms is pushing thousands of federally licensed gun dealers out of business, slashing the number of licenses by nearly half since 1993. The Treasury Secretary is working with anti-gun	legislators to ban the expanding and non-expanding bullets used in virtually all rifle and handgun ammunition. The Center for Disease Control's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control is calling criminal gun violence a	"disease" that more anti-gun laws can "cure." Through trade regulations, the White House banned imports of common, conventional	firearms from Russia - and they plan the same for other countries, as well.	For the first time, the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency has the president's go-ahead to meddle in domestic policy specifically, the right to keep and bear arms. Clinton has even moved to establish a United Nations Task Force on global gun control. If they're doing all that despite our pro-gun majority in Congress, imagine the fallout we'll face if we lose that pro-gun majority and Clinton returns for another term. Imagine the radical policies he'll impose when he longer faces the challenge of reelection. Imagine the consequences if, for four more years, President Clinton fills federal courts - and the U.S. Supreme Court - with judges who share his view that firearms are evil and that citizens can't be trusted with them. Clinton has appointed more than 200 judges to the federal bench. Four more years could mean another 200, along with more Supreme Court nominations, as well. All 435 seats in the U.S. Congress are up for grabs, as well as U.S. Senate seats in 33 states. Our pro-gun allies urgently need our support, but there are other questions you may he considering. In any election, we as voters weigh many overlapping, often competing interests, from jobs and the economy, to taxes and regulation, to deficit reduction and federal expansion. But there's one interest that must supersede all of the others: Freedom. Freedom is the most essential element in our nation's charter and character. It knows no season, or fad or talk-show trend. Just think about it. Crime rises, then falls. The economy heats up, then cools down. But unlike with other issues, with freedom there is no give-and-take. Freedom is fragile - and once lost, nearly impossible to regain, as European nations can well attest. So before you vote on November 5, look at how your freedoms have fared over the past four years. Ask yourself: Do you want four more years of firearms bans, anti-gun political ploys and Clinton's contempt for your Second Amendment freedom? On Election Day, I know what my choice will be. Because when it comes our freedom, the choice is clear.
explanation: The text discusses President Clinton's gun ban, the Brady Bill, and other anti-gun measures, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: ON DECEMBER 2 the President sent to Congress the Budget covering expenditures for the fiscal year 1931. It is gratifying to note that provision has been made for the National Matches and for aid to civilian rifle clubs: $600,000 is recommended for the National Matches and $200,000 for arms and ammunition to members of civilian rifle clubs. With efficient administration the National Matches can be conducted in 1931 for $500,000. The amount of $200,000 is, however, not sufficient for aid to civilian rifle clubs. This amount will aid only 1,600 clubs, and at present there are no less than 65 clubs upon the waiting list and others clamoring for admission. Recently the American Legion and other organizations have signified a desire to become actively interested in rifle-shooting. This activity will produce many additional clubs. This item in the Budget covering aid to civilians should undoubtedly be increased by approximately $50,000 to care for the actual and anticipated increase in interest. The minimum amount needed is $250,000. The Budget is commonly called the President's Budget, but it is your Budget as well. It is considered and passed upon by your representatives - men who have been sent to Washington to speak and act for you and to do your bidding. If you have not already expressed yourself to your representatives upon this subject, they can not know how you feel about it. Every shooter believes in national defense. The National Matches and aid to civilian rifle clubs are two of the foundation stones In the great national structure of preparedness. Your representatives have a right to know how you feel about these things In order that they may properly represent you when the items are under consideration, write and urge them to appropriate $500,000 for the National Matches and to increase the item for rifles and ammunition to $250,000. Let them know that you are interested in these Items. Act upon this matter immediately and do not wait for others. Make the Budget your Budget.
explanation: The text discusses the budget for the National Matches and civilian rifle clubs, but does not address gun regulation.

text: IF you are like most gun owners, you live surrounded in part or entirely by people who know little about firearms and may care less, or even be afraid of them. Your big opportunity to introduce these people to firearms sports is coming on National Hunting and Fishing Day, Sept. 28, provided you and your friends plan ahead now. Through activities you can help set up on this national day, you can not only expand your circle of neighbors and acquaintances interested in firearms, but reinforce your own possession and use of guns for sporting purposes by enlisting more citizens in the ranks of gun owners. In very many of the nooks and crannies that make this nation, there are clubs and local groups planning NHF Day Activities. Almost 3000 events took place last year. Join them in their effort this year. If you live where nothing is happening, you can make something happen by suggesting an event to an existing organization. If there is no group, you can start one-enlist a newspaper columnist, a radio station, a sporting goods store, and your fellow shooters and send for a publicity kit to The National Shooting Sports Foundation, 1075 Post Road, Riverside, Conn. 06878. The kit costs $3. Your $3 investment could be a very important factor in maintaining the health of shooting sports where you live.
explanation: The text promotes National Hunting and Fishing Day and encourages participation in related activities, but does not address gun regulation.

text: As another public service activity, the National Rifle Association of America has opened its new firearms museum. It is located in the beautiful NRA headquarters on Rhode Island Avenue at Sixteenth Street in northwest Washington D.C. It will be open to the public every day of the year, except Christmas Day, from 10 o'clock in the morning until 4 o'clock in the afternoon. While there are many different types of museums, ranging from modest places for the display of curios to imposing shrines for the housing of great arrays of treasures, they have the primary function to assemble and care for material worthy of exhibition and to present it to the public for education and enjoyment. The NRA Museum contains a collection which presents a complete picture of the development and history of firearms. It includes all classes from the primitive weapons to the highly specialized arms of today. One display portrays the development of firearms by ignition system from the hand cannon through metallic-cartridge breechloaders. Another display shows the milestones in arms development from early breech-loading cartridge arms to the present. Current and obsolete U.S. and foreign metallic cartridges and shot-shells are on exhibit. The art of gunmaking is prevented by examples of guns with an exceptionally high order of workmanship, finish, and ornamentation. There are all kinds of firearms, both domestic and foreign. They include rifles and carbines, pistols and revolvers, as well as shotguns and airguns. We Americans are proud of our history, and no tools have done more to shape that history than firearms in the hands of our courageous ancestors. We can see in firearms the ingenuity of the inventor and the craftsmanship of the metalworker, the wood-worker, and the engraver. We can let our thoughts drift in history down through the days of the flintlock and the Kentucky rifle and recall great events in which they played a vital role - Lexington, Concord, Yorktown, New Orleans. We can turn to the great westward migration and the early days of the pioneer with their long Pennsylvania-made rifles, their Hawken plains rifles, their Sharps buffalo guns, their old trap-door Springfields, and eventually the Winchesters, the Remingtons, the Colts, and similar arms. As a nation we are growing up, and with this maturity we are developing a greater interest and pride in our history. The NRA Museum will help to spread historical information and encourage historical inquiry. It is more than just an interesting place to visit. It is, in fact, an institution where the firearms themselves tell the story of the history of firearms.
explanation: The text describes the NRA's new firearms museum and its historical exhibits, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Except for US. income tax returns, few Federal requirements impose a bigger mountain of paperwork on the American people than the 1968 Gun Control Act. By best estimates, this act requires the detailed recording of 30 million retail transactions every year on .22 rimfire ammunition alone. Every time anyone wants so much as a box of 50 of these cartridges from a Federally licensed dealer, he must identify himself to the dealer's satisfaction by a driver's license or equivalent means. The dealer must then enter in a bound record, to be kept at least two years, the buyer's name, address, birth date and mode of identification, plus the date of transaction, quantity and caliber of ammunition bought, and the manufacturer of it. While Congress exempted rifle and shotgun ammunition from this redtape procedure in 1969, the requirement still applies on all .22 rimfire ammunition, as well as handgun ammunition, because .22's can be used in handguns. Involved in this maze of paperwork are, by National Shooting Sports Foundation estimates, some three billion rounds of .22's a year constituting 60% of all ammunition sales. Aside from helping to snow under a country already cluttered with more government paperwork than probably any other in the world, it is hard to see what use this detailed record-keeping serves. No one apparently believes that it has made a serious dent in crime. Elsewhere in this issue, we discuss the major role played by .22's in a variety of outdoor sports and activities. As we point out, the .22 is no toy. It should be used cautiously under proper conditions conducive to safety. But if it is no toy, neither is it in itself an evil thing - nor a thing that can or should be controlled by intensive bookkeeping. The House of Representatives voted 246 to 59 last year to end the record-keeping requirement on .22's. The Senate Judiciary Committee, which received the House bill, approved it. But that session of Congress ended before the bill could be passed, so it died with adjournment. Fresh bills to exempt .22's were promptly introduced this year. There are now 22 of them in the House and two in the Senate. One group of five such House bills (H R. 1677, 4260, 4261, 4262 and 5271) by Rep. Robert L. F. Sikes (1st Dist., Fla.) has been co-sponsored by 75 other Congressmen. In the Senate, S. 144 by Sen. Gale McGee (Wyo.) has 37 co-sponsors from 25 States. All of these bills are considered revenue measures, as they involve firearms taxes, and have therefore been referred to the Senate Finance Committee or House Ways and Means Committee. Approval is expected in the late spring or early summer. Whenever it comes, its supporters can be sure of one thing. It will be welcomed by a majority of the American public.
explanation: The text discusses the 1968 Gun Control Act and proposed legislation to exempt .22 rimfire ammunition from its record-keeping requirements, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: As I write this column just a few short hours after the close of the polls on Nov 8., I feel like the perfectly healthy soul who has just passed every test known to medical science but doesn't feel like celebrating because he's just come down with a painful toothache. I guess the word "bittersweet" applies. Thanks in great part to the strength and determination of NRA's membership, a pro-gun President-elect is about to hold his first news conference. His opponent is back in Massachusetts. Nebraskans are celebrating a 65% to 35% voter approval of a Constitutional amendment guaranteeing the Cornhuskers' right to keep and bear arms. And, in political contests too numerous to mention here - ILA will give you the particulars later - NRA supporters have swept to victory throughout the country. The one nagging setback that brings the pain? The defeat of the Maryland Committee Against the Gun Ban's attempt to overturn legislation passed by the General Assembly banning certain unnamed handguns. This was, of course, a loss for all of the people of Maryland. The Assembly's search for an answer to crime control was badly misdirected, as such attempts always are, and will in due time result in both abject failure and a further erosion of the people's faith in their lawmakers. The voters were obviously swayed by what the Governor, his Attorney General and various police superintendents said the law INTENDED to do rather than what it actually said. With the help of the political establishment, the police hierarchy and virtually all of the TV stations and newspapers, they stonewalled and misrepresented the definition of the legislation. In this campaign, more than in any other in which we've participated, most of the electronic and print media dropped all pretense at fair, objective reporting and aggressively supported the gun ban at every opportunity. The Washington Post, for example, editorialized every day for 10 days prior to the election. Some of its diatribes accused us of lying and of trying to buy the election while others were simply free copy for the	opposition's statements. Imagine the value of this "free" advertising and know that it was significantly greater than anything our Committee could afford to purchase. But, as the old song says, every cloud has a silver lining and here are some facts that will cause you to respect and congratulate the men and women of NRA's Maryland membership, their Committee's heroic Chairman Fred Grisser and thousands more whom we all salute: A state affiliate which historically has suffered from a degree of lethargy was transformed into an excellent and enthusiastic campaign force. Thousands of new people have have been recruited into the fold. From a low point of 17% of the electorate favoring our side when the campaign began, we rose to more than 42% on election day. Thus, we were successful in getting 42% of the people to read the law and to agree with us that it was not restricted to any single category of handguns. 630,000 citizens voted for our position in political environment in which we were the only people asking for their support. Seventeen of the 23 counties in Maryland sided with our members. The anti gun groups and the Washington/Baltimore media want to belive that the Maryland vote will result in "a ripple effect in other states" (the reporters' words). I believe that as long as the National Rifle Association stands up for gun owners' rights, wherever the challenges surface, serious politicians will think carefully about supporting worthless legislative agendas that will earn them the united, totally committed opposition of our membership. Remember, Maryland is one of only seven states in the country that does not have a Constitutional provision guaranteeing its citizens the right to keep and bear arms. I know that I speak for us all when I say that our Marylanders fought too courageous a fight to let it end here. This battle is over but we will be back, Maryland. Bet on it!
explanation: The text discusses the defeat of a referendum to overturn a handgun ban in Maryland and the broader implications for gun rights, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: IN April, 1940, we commented editorially under the above title with regard to the Garand (M-1) rifle and the M-2 (1906) ammunition. After pointing out certain facts, and certain questions which were as a result raised, we said: "We have no partisan interest, no 'fish to fry,' no 'backs to scratch.' We only feel that matters have reached a point where someone should have the courage to bring the discussion out of by-ways that seem to lead nowhere onto the highway which leads to frank, friendly, constructive effort in behalf of the nation's efficient defense." The questions which we raised at that time regarding the wisdom of abandoning the modern M-1 ammunition and returning to the once-obsolete 1906 ammunition, now designated M-2, still remain the subject of speculation and debate. Here is an open question which, unfortunately, may not be determined until tested in the impartial laboratory of another war. Fortunately, however, some of the other questions - those relative to the M-1 (Garand) rifle - have been answered in the year just passed. Changes in manufacturing specifications and methods have resulted in a marked improvement in the Garand rifle. Upon the strength of its use by a variety of troops under a variety of conditions, it now seems proper to say that the Garand rifles currently coming off the production line are as accurate at all ranges as are the production-model Springfields which they are replacing. As far as can be determined outside of the acid test of actual war, the Garand appears to be a sturdy, dependable weapon, pretty nearly - although not quite - the equal of the manually operated Springfield in this respect. It is doubtful if a semi-automatic weapon of this type can ever be placed upon the same level of war-time mass production as is possible for a manually operated arm. Development of special tools has, however, materially increased the production rate at Springfield, and if the Government is willing to erect the necessary facilities - and always provided that we are granted the time in which to erect the facilities, it is now evident that the Garand rifle can be manufactured on a production basis. In extensive tests recently completed by the Marine Corps, the Garand rifle clearly indicated that it was the best of the semi-automatics submitted for test, and it plainly showed its improved accuracy. We expect to carry in our May issue an article, or the first of a series of articles, written by a Marine Corps Officer and released with the approval of the Marine Corps, reporting on these tests in detail. In our editorial of April, 1940, we concluded with the paragraph: "In the interest of America may we all-officers and enlisted men, civilian riflemen and manufacturers who are qualified to speak - may we all have the courage to be frank and the good sense to be gentlemen and sportsmen!" It is in that spirit that we are glad to report that the Garand rifle has now satisfactorily answered most of the questions which its own performance of a year ago raised. It is in that same spirit that we say we believe there still remains an open question as to the wisdom of discarding the splendid M-1 cartridge in favor of the ammunition which proved unsatisfactory to American soldiers operating on American tactical principles in the last great war.
explanation: The text discusses the history and performance of the Garand (M-1) rifle and its ammunition, but does not address gun regulation.

text: My good personal friend Jimmie Rutledge served in World War II and in Korea, and then for 22 years as a police officer in Berkeley, Calif. He met his end suddenly at 5 a.m. June 16 - from a bullet. He was the second police officer shot dead in his area in three weeks. As one of Jimmie's best friends, I feel aggrieved - but not at guns. You see, Jimmie and his fellow officer were both killed with their own guns, snatched from them by maniacs. Jimmie's murderer went berserk on LSD. He had been on the drug for weeks before the tragedy, police said. After killing Sergeant Rutledge, who had answered a routine call reporting "a prowler," this LSD maniac shot and killed a four-year-old girl in her crib and attempted to murder his own wife, but ran out of ammunition. When the killer rushed outside, bullets from other police guns cut him down forever. Jimmie left his wife, Betty, and children James, Cynthia and Pamela - a fine family, bereft of a father who had served his country in war and his community in what passes for peace. Jimmie and I used to go to matches back when he was single, and I taught him the basics of handgun shooting and marksmanship. But he never had a chance against a man maddened by LSD. No gun "control" law could have prevented this tragedy. The drug control laws didn't prevent it, either. An absolute prohibition on firearms in Berkeley couldn't have stopped it. Seven hundred police officers attended Jimmie's funeral. I doubt that more than a handful of them think that a gun control law could have saved him. What we have got to accomplish goes deeper than simply "passing a law." It has got to reach the people who break the law, whether they abuse drugs or guns or any other inanimate but potentially lethal object. What else can I say, except that Jimmie is gone and many of us miss him? - K. Lambert Kirk (Note: Kirk Lambert Kirk is a practicing San Francisco attorney, an NRA Director, an Expert Pistol Marksman, and Pistol Commissioner of the San Francisco Olympic Club. In publishing this tribute to his friend, The American Rifleman makes an exception to its editorial policy in recognition of the heroic service of U.S. law enforcement officers everywhere. Views such as those of K. Lambert Kirk stand out in strong contrast with those of Mayor Lindsay, of New York City, who turned the occasion of the funeral of a policeman shot there into a public criticism of the US. as "the only country with no meaningful gun control - a gun-slinging country." Mayor Lindsay's solution is of course to disarm everybody. Everybody? - The Editor.)
explanation: The text is a tribute to a fallen police officer and discusses the inability of gun control laws to prevent his death, but does not address gun regulation.

text: NRA Benefactor Member F.D. Ward, Jr, of Orlando Fla., gave me the theme for this column. "Guns of the Anti-Gunners," in a letter he wrote to President Joe Foss. While reading my copy of his letter, I was reminded of the number of times people of fame, wealth or position have opposed NRA on the subject of the Second Amendment, often times stridently and irresponsibly, while retaining unto themselves rights they were more than willing to take from us. The most recent example of this "some are more equal than others" hypocrisy is perhaps the loudest of them all, columnist Carl Rowan. I don't have to tell you of the immense amount of publicity given to that anti-gun guru for his unlawful possession of a handgun or of the interest it has sparked among our membership. We've received all sorts of suggestions as to how best to treat the matter, the most popular being that we include him in "The Armed Citizen." The Editor of that noteworthy page correctly pointed out that those news reports involve law-abiding citizens using legally owned firearms in a proper, exemplary manner. Obviously the Editor felt that Rowan did not fall within this category. While this incident is fresh in our minds let it not obscure equally twisted reasoning on the part of other notables who've told us to do as they said, and not as they did while they led the anti-gun crusade. An incomplete list would include the following: former San Francisco Mayor Dianne Feinstein who announced a city handgun ban and then turned in one of her two handguns (the small caliber). District of Columbia Mavor Marion Barry, who owned a .38 Spl. revolver but gave it in favor of armed bodyguards. Former New York Mayor John Lindsay, advocate of restrictive gun laws while holding a concealed carry permit. New York Times publisher Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, who also holds a permit to carry a concealed handgun while his newspaper prostrates itself in favor of any restrictions on such firearms. Otis Chandler, publisher of the Los Angeles Times, a famous worldwide hunter whose paper marches lock-step with Sulzberger's on our issue. Actress Jennifer O'Neill who told a New York court that she was "very much against guns" and could not positively identify the gun with which she accidentally shot herself. Senator Ted Kennedy who defended the unlawful carrying of guns by his bodyguard into the Russell Senate Office Building. About-to-be former Congressman Mario Biaggi, once the House of Representative's leading anti-gunner, had to turn in two handguns after he was convicted of a felony. Remember Morton Grove, Ill.? The mayor's wife became a member of the couurt in order to lawfully own a handgun despite that town's gun ban. BUT she had a police officer obtain the pistol for her in violation of the state's three day waiting period and also in violation of the Firearms Owner's Identification Card provision. And how about some of those police chiefs who apper in Handgun Control, Inc.'s ads? While they seek to diarm us, I'm curious as to just what they carry in their service holsters. San Jose Chief Joe McNamara admits to keeping a handgun at home for protection because of threats he claims to have received. How do you like this quote of McNamara's, "As much as I oppose the average person's having a gun, I recognize that some people have a legitimate need to own one. A wealthy corporate executive who fears his family might get kidnapped is one such person. A Hollywood celebrity who has to protect himself from kooks is another." How about the little guy, Joe? Shouldn't the poor and not-so-famous have an equal chance to protect their families and themselves? The point of this parade of horribles is obvious. In order to advance their unholy cause, these notables and their allies are willing to dissemble, cover up, exaggerate and misrepresent most of the legitimate reasons that exist in law and in life for the overwhelming majority of law-abiding Americans to keep and bear arms. As with some once popular preachers and politicians whose credibility faded once their actions became public, so, too, should the influence of these arch foes crumble once their gun-owning habits are publicized.
explanation: The text discusses the hypocrisy of anti-gun advocates who own firearms themselves and the NRA's role in exposing this, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: "We start therefore with a strong presumption that the Second Amendment right is exercised individually and belongs to all Americans." - U.S. Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, June 26, 2008. For all of us, as members of the National Rifle Association and for millions of other Americans, that pronouncement by the U.S. Supreme Court is perhaps the most important we will ever read or hear. It is a vindication of what we and a majority of Americans have always known. The media would have gun owners believe that with this landmark decision, the fight is over. The truth is, it is just beginning. This is the opening salvo in a step-by-step process of bringing relief to people all over this country who have been deprived of access to Second Amendment freedom. NRA is filing lawsuits in places like Chicago and its suburbs, and in San Francisco, where gun-ban statutes still block the doorway to freedom. With this monumental decision, we will also be fighting to restore rights through the legislative process, in Congress and in state legislatures to bring statutes into line with this critical doctrine of Constitutional law. The Second Amendment must never be walled off by the elite so that only the rich and famous or politically connected can access this freedom, while average citizens are told, "You're flat out of luck." In reading this landmark decision striking down the District of Columbia's three-decades old gun-ban, it has come to me time and again that this victory for freedom is not just about the culmination of decades of deep legal and historical scholarship or about the brilliant legal work of many individuals ... it's also about raw electoral politics. This Supreme Court victory is about you, your families and friends-your votes - especially in the last two presidential elections. And this remarkable decision is about President George W. Bush keeping his faith with us that he would appoint justices - like Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Samuel Alito - who interpret our Constitutional rights as they were intended by our founding fathers. Justice Scalia's 64-page Second Amendment opinion was remarkably clear and answered key, fundamental questions. Joined in the 5-4 majority by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Alito, Clarence Thomas and Anthony Kennedy, the court concluded: "... we hold that the District's ban on handgun possession in the home violates the Second Amendment, as does its prohibition against rendering any lawful firearm in the home operable for the purpose of immediate self-defense." On the utility of handguns, he wrote, "... the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon ... and a complete prohibition of their use is invalid ..." On future Second Amendment cases, Scalia was unequivocal, "... whatever else it leaves to future evaluation, it surely elevates above all other interests the right of law-abiding, responsible citizens to use arms in defense of hearth and home." That bedrock belief was ridiculed by Justice John Paul Stevens as an "overwrought and novel description of the Second Amendment." Stevens, in his dissent, said the right was solely "to maintain a well-regulated militia." And he said the framers of the Constitution "never evidenced the slightest interest in limiting any legislature's authority to regulate private civilian uses of firearms [as with D.C.'s ban]. Specifically, there is no indication that the Framers of the Amendment intended to enshrine the common-law right of self-defense in the Constitution." Stevens was joined in dissent by Justices David Souter, Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer. For the majority, Scalia fired back, "... it is not the role of this Court to pronounce the Second Amendment extinct." But consider this. Except for one vote, that is exactly what a Stevens majority would have done. But for one vote, total bans on firearm ownership would have gotten the imprimatur of the high court, and such laws would have metastasized through the efforts of New York billionaire Mayor Mike Bloomberg's cabal of big city mayors and his fellow globalist billionaire, George Soros. And that brings me back to electoral politics. This November, with the sure bet that there will be two, perhaps three vacancies on the U.S. Supreme Court in the near future, we face a clear choice. If Barack Obama takes the White House, he will nominate enemies of the Second Amendment. That is a sure thing. John McCain - on the other hand - sees Justices Scalia, Alito, Roberts and Thomas as models for the kind of jurists he would appoint. No matter what other issues might intervene, there is nothing more important than maintaining or increasing the pro-Second Amendment majority on the high court this November. The court's decision was a great moment in American history, but it shows how fragile freedom is and how vigilant we must always be, each and every day, to protect it.
explanation: The text discusses the Supreme Court's decision on the Second Amendment and the NRA's ongoing legal and legislative efforts to protect gun rights, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: The International Olympic Committee maintains that it can find no place for smallbore events for women shooters in the famous Olympic Games. The professed reason is that the Olympics are overgrown and, they say, already involve far too many people. Yet the IOC reportedly yielded to pressure and included women's basketball and team handball events in the Olympics for the first time after rejecting the women's smallbore events. Women have participated in events of their own in the Olympics since the 1920's if not earlier. Current competitions for women include track and field, swimming and diving, archery, fencing, skating, gymnastics, skiing, rowing, basketball and volley ball. There are 15 such separate programs, some including a dozen or more individual matches. Women are also eligible to compete as persons with men in shooting as well as in yachting, horseback riding and canoeing. It required a strenuous effort of U.S. Olympic officials, including the late Franklin L. Orth, then NRA Executive Vice President, to pry open the Olympics to women shooters at all, and that was managed only in 1967. What The National Rifle Association of America and other backers of women's events propose now is simply to add smallbore prone and three-position matches for women, plus air rifle and air pistol events for all. Against the vast panoply of the Olympic Games it seems like asking very little.
explanation: The text discusses the exclusion of women's smallbore shooting events from the Olympics and the NRA's efforts to include them, but does not address gun regulation.

text: In the quarter-century just ended, the United Stales has engaged in three no-win wars - conflicts in which we fought with one hand tied. They proved tragic, costly and traumatic to our nation. Two of them, in Korea and Vietnam, are past. But our third no-win war, perhaps the most important of all, still rages. This third war is being fought, not in the distant Orient by U.S armed forces, but in the streets around us by an equally heroic army of law enforcement officers. There are painful similarities in these three no-win struggles. Just as the country at large left it to a few hundred thousands of its sons to carry on the shooting wars against Communism overseas, so does the American public leave it largely to the police to wage war on crime with relatively little general support. Just as the Korean and Vietnam conflicts were limited in their scope, if not their deadliness and ferocity, by diplomatic considerations, so is the war to protect the American public from rampant crime hampered by the manner in which some courts free criminals who then repeat their crimes. On Lake Erie in the War of 1812. U.S. Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry defeated a British fleet und then messaged: "We have met the enemy and they are ours. . . ." In other words, their ships were sunk or captured and would not have to be fought again. But in our homefront war. the public enemy, or some part of it, virtually uses the courts for "rest and recreation" before resuming attacks on the American public again and again. How police morale remains so high is a wonder. In our two no-win wars abroad our strategic moves were severely limited by global diplomacy There was always deep concern in Washington, D.C., that an unrestrained U.S. offensive might unleash a nuclear war. Those who have in effect left our police to battle under a handicap in defending the home front can offer no such excuse. While the possibility of nuclear gangsterism cannot be completely discounted, there is no immediate and evident threat of nuclear devastation such as haunted overseas wars. The two no-win wars abroad cost us 79,792 Americans killed in combat. The no-win war at home has resulted in 858 law enforcement officers being killed in the period 1964-73. Some 77% of those identified as assailants of the slain officers had records of previous arrests, according to the FBI Uniform Crime Reporting Center. Some 59% had been convicted of crime before. Nearly two-thirds of these were free, at the time the officers were killed, through parole or pardon. That is why our national campaign against crime, into which the Federal government is pouring millions through the Law Enforcement Assistance Administration, needs court and public support if it is to succeed. Our third no-win war is the one we can worst afford - because it strikes us right here on the home front.
explanation: The text discusses the challenges of law enforcement in combating crime and the similarities to wartime struggles, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Between now and the November elections, Bill Clinton will do everything in his power to elect a rubber-stamp Congress in lock-step with his dream legacy - the swift destruction of the Second Amendment. And he will use every corruption of executive power to elect his successor - Al Gore - to carry out that legacy. The Constitution forbids Bill Clinton from running for another term, but he is running - in the form of his clone, Al Gore, whom he called "the most qualified person in my lifetime to seek this job." They are one and the same ... in their deep disdain for the Second Amendment, in their corruption of government and in their twisting of the truth. And they are the same in their reckless disregard for the prudent enforcement of existing Federal laws against violent criminals with guns. I keep hearing the whispers of Washington insiders that NRA should ignore Bill Clinton - that he's history, a lame duck. Then I listen to NRA members - who know the danger is real until the moment we elect a Second Amendment President, and send a Second Amendment majority to Congress. Ask rank-and-file gun owners in Colorado whether the danger from Bill Clinton has diminished. In a tasteless, shameless political trip - a week before the anniversary of the Columbine tragedy - Clinton flew into Colorado to lobby for passage of a ballot initiative to accomplish sweeping anti-firearms strictures that had been rejected by the Colorado legislature. Clinton used Air Force One to fly in the new head of Handgun Control, Inc., former Maryland Congressman Michael Barnes, to lobby the Colorado public on gun restrictions. This was Bill Clinton and HCI hand-in-hand on a taxpayer-funded trip to gore the rights of taxpayers they would disarm. At a state bill signing in Maryland, where beleaguered firearms owners face an insidious mandatory "safety lock" law, Clinton used the occasion as a presidential pulpit to demand that other states follow suit. The Associated Press reported, "With his gun bill stuck on Capitol Hill, President Clinton is taking to the road to encourage a burgeoning move in the states to deal with the firearms safety questions that Congress has not." Using the Office of the President for purely political purposes to the detriment of gun owners is nothing new. Over the past year, a major part of the president's time has been spent in blatantly political trips to raise funds in private residences in fat-cat $10,000-a-plate dinners and in purely partisan fundraising meetings. Among the private residence money-klatches reported on The White House website were trips to Cincinnati, Ohio, where Clinton raised political money at the home of one of the key trial lawyers in the suits to destroy the firearms industry. Clinton came away with big bucks to line the political coffers of his anti-gun, hand-groomed candidates for Congress. At The White House website, when you type in a search for "NRA," most of the documents called up are Clinton speeches to political fundraisers - making the White House website a fundraising site. At every appearance - falsely claimed as official business - Clinton always speaks poisonously about the NRA. Using taxpayer funds, Clinton is raising millions of dollars to elect an HCI Congress. NRA is his central whipping boy. Is lame-duck Clinton still dangerous? Ask anybody involved in the lawful, regulated commerce of firearms whether the misuse of power by Bill Clinton has diminished. The lawsuit extortion of one company and the attempted extortion of all major handgun manufacturers and their chain of commerce has no basis in law. Yet under the direction of Al Gore and Bill Clinton, the resources of several Federal agencies are bearing down to crush an entire industry. Leading the way is the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) headed by Andrew Cuomo who reportedly is being groomed as Al Gore's running mate. Under our Constitutional system of checks and balances, the executive branch can only do what Congress authorizes. And an executive agency can only carry out an authorized function if Congress provides the appropriations. The Congress never authorized HUD to create new "gun controls" through coercion. The Congress never authorized HUD to conduct gun "buybacks" and never appropriated one thin dime for that. The Congress never authorized HUD to dictate the brand of firearms that law officers must buy under no-bid insider deals with one single manufacturer. It's happening. If this is Al Gore's reinvention of government, it's spelled "C-O-R-R-U-P-T-I-O-N" of government - all through the back door.
