Imagine what life would be like with an HCI-controlIed, gunowner-hating Congress willing to give similar power on a vast scale fueled by unlimited taxpayer funding. Imagine if the Federal Consumer Product Safety Commission were empowered to ban guns on a fast track. If Al Gore is elected and if Bill Clinton gets the Congress he is campaigning for, our rights as free Americans will be under constant fire. Each of us must work harder than Bill Clinton and Al Gore between now and the coming elections. We must deliver votes - ours and the votes of our friends, families and neighbors. We must prepare for November. We must educate every voter we can. We must get pledges for their support. Get friends and relatives registered to vote. The future of our firearms rights and, indeed, the Bill of Rights depends on what we do. Nothing less than the Second Amendment - our freedom to live under the protection of those rights - is at stake. Using taxpayer funds, Clinton is raising millions of dollars to elect an HCI Congress. NRA is his central whipping boy.
explanation: The text discusses President Clinton's and Al Gore's anti-gun agenda, including lawsuits and executive actions targeting the firearm industry, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: A few months ago when I warned about New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg's declaration of war on the Second Amendment, his demands for more gun control were just that. But today - with rapidly growing support from other urban mayors, suburban blue-state elites and an unquestioning media blitz - Bloomberg's campaign has grown to a full-blown attempt to overthrow the pro-Second Amendment majority in Congress this November. Repeated hundreds of times in the media, Bloomberg's big lie is summed up by a Christian Science Monitor article that claims: "Despite tough gun laws against guns in many cities and states, lax Federal rules do not prevent the sale of handguns across state lines." Nothing could be further from the truth. Start with the fact that any interstate sale of handguns outside licensed Federal dealers is a crime. Then add to that the host of tough Federal felony provisions covering any aspect of criminal, black-market commerce - from acquisition through "straw sales," to possession, to interstate transport, to illegal sales, to "gun trafficking" - already against Federal law in every corner of the nation. Bloomberg knows it. But enforcing Federal law against criminals involved in gun trafficking does not serve his purpose. All this is a ruse, pure and simple. In large measure Bloomberg's new national campaign against gun owners and the pro-Second Amendment majority in Congress is a colossal tantrum over the enactment of Federal restrictions on lawsuits designed to shut down the law-abiding firearm industry. In spite of that landmark law forbidding such punitive, predatory legal actions, Bloomberg has pressed forward with his latest New York City lawsuit before Brooklyn Federal Judge Jack B. Weinstein, who has ruled he will hear the case in spite of the lawsuit ban. This is the latest action before that judge, with major support from fellow billionaire George Soros, the Brady Center and the Violence Policy Center. In seeking retribution for the lawsuit ban by overthrowing the pro-Second Amendment congressional majority, Bloomberg would take great comfort in seeing NRA "F"-rated Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) as Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives and long-time gun-confiscation advocate John Conyers (D-Mich.) as chairman of the all-powerful Judiciary Committee. The same would be true were Bloomberg to get his way with the U.S. Senate. It's not hard to imagine what his ideological mentors, Teddy Kennedy (D-Mass.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.), would do were they to take control of the Senate Judiciary Committee. They would fill Bloomberg's legislative orders. Much is being made in the media about Bloomberg's Republican party affiliation. But in fact, media magnate Bloomberg, ranked as one of the richest men in the world, became a Republican only shortly before declaring his candidacy for mayor of New York City, an office he took after spending $87 million of his own funds. In buying his second term, he reportedly spent in excess of $84 million, with $34 million for broadcast ads alone. Until he ran for mayor, Bloomberg had been a lifelong leftist member of the party of gun-ban leaders - Al Gore, Chuck Schumer and Carolyn McCarthy (D-N.Y.) - whose election campaigns he has actively and financially supported since he switched parties. Recently, the New York Post reported that he could have influence on Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton's re-election campaign saying, "many political insiders have speculated he'll cross party lines to endorse her." Republicans, especially those who make up the pro-Second Amendment majority in Congress, should recognize this powerful adversary as one who would destroy what they stand for and remove them from positions of leadership. As part of the urban mayors' litigation and political war on gun rights, the Brady Campaign is a Bloomberg adjunct, with another anti-Second Amendment politician, former Fort Wayne, Ind., Mayor Paul Helmke taking the helm of that gun-ban group. As with Bloomberg, the media has been smugly repeating the fact that Helmke is a Republican. In terms of safeguarding Second Amendment rights, NRA is and always has been politically bipartisan. We support Democrats, and we support Republicans. The only thing that counts is performance. And Helmke, like Bloomberg, is an "F" many times over. Like our successful fight to keep globalist gun-ban billionaire George Soros from buying the White House for John Kerry in the last presidential election, Bloomberg's war on our Second Amendment rights can only be won by ordinary Americans standing up against an elitist who believes his money can buy anything - including our Freedom. This coming election is key to saving our rights from his clutches. Register to vote. Vote early if you can. Get your friends to vote for pro-Second Amendment congressional and senatorial candidates. Make sure that the members of Bloomberg's dream team - the F-Troop - don't become his powerful water-carriers.
explanation: The text discusses Mayor Michael Bloomberg's campaign against gun rights, including lawsuits and political efforts to overturn pro-Second Amendment majorities, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: February marks the birth anniversaries of two of America's greatest Presidents, George Washington and Abraham Lincoln. Both of these titanic leaders reached their zenith of greatness while guiding our country through wars which could have killed off the nation at birth or before maturity. Both knew firearms, for military and for sporting purposes. George Washington spent nearly a quarter of his life under arms. When he died at 67, he had soldiered for 15 and a half years. When peace and leisure permitted, he hunted constantly. Hunting was perhaps the favorite and foremost recreation of the Father of His Country. Abraham Lincoln's numerous biographies note that he "hunted," that he "shot wild turkey," and that he served in the militia in the Black Hawk War. His interest in firearms, especially in military weapons efficient enough to shorten the Civil War. led him personally to test-fire and approve the Spencer repeater, the first magazine cartridge arm extensively used by U.S. Forces. Lincoln as commander-in-chief directed probably the biggest rifleman's war in the Western hemisphere, in which by far the highest percentage of casualties were caused by infantry bullets. Like Washington, he fully recognized the role of firearms. For one man, they created a new nation. For the other, they held it together. So America was fortunate that both of these heroic wartime leaders of classic stature had a thorough grasp and understanding of firearms. But the wars themselves, in 1775 and 1861, what did they start over? In 1775, was it the Stamp Tax, the quartering of British regulars in the homes of American colonials, "taxation without representation." or what? In 1861, was it the Fugitive Slave Act, "Bleeding Kansas," the tariff issue between industrial North and agricultural South, or what? What actually turned each clash of words into a "shooting war"? The answer in both instances is very nearly the same. In 1775 the shooting began when the British, after methodically disarming every individual American who left Boston, marched a column of redcoats from Boston to Concord. Mass., to seize the arms of American militia stored there. In 1861, the first shots were fired over whether a fort in the harbor of Charleston, S.C., should be evacuated and in effect disarmed. Both wars, then, sprang in their full-blown form from efforts to disarm Americans who would not be disarmed. Whenever anyone stops to ask himself what will make Americans fighting mad, he might do well to consider 1775 and 1861. Perhaps, on the anniversaries of Washington and Lincoln, that is as timely a thought as any.
explanation: The text discusses the historical significance of firearms in the lives of Presidents Washington and Lincoln, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Much has been said during the past few years about the growing dependence of the average American on his government; about the increasing willingness of Americans to sell their birthright of personal liberty for the mess of pottage offered by governmental administrative controls; about the dangers inherent in the creation of a legislature which rides into office on the coattails of a brilliant leader, coupled with a judiciary appointed largely by that same dominating character, and an executive group and subordinate bureaucracy owing its daily bread to the one master. Much has been said; but, too often, what should have been coolly logical, constructive discussion degenerated into hotheaded argument and personal attacks. Largely for this reason, most Americans gradually turned their attention to less explosive subjects of conversation. But even to those students of government who recognized the trend, its extent came as a shock when revealed by the sudden death of their great leader, Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Said a soldier, peering through the pickets of the White House fence, "I can't realize he is gone. Why, he is the only President I can remember." Said a middle-aged housewife, with tears in her eyes, "I am all confused. I am frightened. I feel as though I have lost the provider out of my family." Said a painter, a thrifty, hard-working naturalized American, "I can't seem to get on with my job. Many things he did that I did not like; but what are we going to do now that he is gone?" Typical of millions, these Americans unconsciously symbolized the dependence, not on democratic processes but on one man, which had unwittingly come to dominate the minds of a people engaged even then in their bloodiest struggle for independence! Over the radio, commentators, caught off guard by the suddenness of the tragedy, repeated the refrain hour after hour: "Our great leader is dead; there is none to take his place. We must close our ranks, pull together, pray together, trust now to ourselves and to ordinary men to see the Nation through its crisis." Apparently, not one of them saw, for the moment, anything but danger in the fact that the American people must now take an interest in their government, must now pull together, must now pray together, must now make democracy work to win the war and the peace! Not one seemed to realize the incongruity of fearing the ordinary man. the plain, God-fearing leader, in a democracy founded by and for such people. Certainly Franklin Roosevelt's death was a great tragedy. Certainly he had earned a place in the hearts of the common people of the world. Certainly he was one of the masterful leaders of all time. What is written here is not intended and must not be construed as any reflection on a captain departed, or any disparagement of his amazing record. But America is, after all, a democracy and the only way for a democracy to continue in full vigor is through the active interest of even one of its citizens in the functions of its government. When President Truman said in his message to Congress, "The responsibility of the great states is to serve and not to dominate the world . . . We shall need an abiding faith in the people ... I ask only to be a good and faithful servant of my Lord and my people," he spoke the language of those who created America's democratic heritage. He showed then the faith that makes democracy work - the spirit that made America for two centuries the Mecca of courageous men seeking personal liberty. In that spirit, with a government of law and not of men, with faith in the common sense of the common man, Harry Truman and the American people will go on to their greater destiny.
explanation: The text discusses the dangers of dependence on government and the importance of individual liberty, but does not address gun regulation.

text: "Japan's (gun) laws seem to pay off." "Gun control laws seem to work fairly well in other countries." Those are quotations from a weekly newspaper published by a private firm for public school children in Ohio and elsewhere. They are part of a "lesson" embodying anti-gun statistics and attitudes. The "other countries" mentioned are, of course, Japan and England - never all of Great Britain, which includes Scotland with its higher homicide rate. Both are compact island empires with highly homogeneous, orderly populations, quite unlike the U.S. - or Mexico - or Russia. The educational publication says nothing about neighboring Mexico, which has the strictest gun laws in North America and a homicide rate 2 and a half times that of the U.S. Needless to say, the publication says nothing about Soviet Russia, where rigid gun controls recently failed to prevent an assassination inside the Kremlin and a triple murder by a gunman who made his own ammunition. The Soviet gun laws are almost perfect from an anti-gun viewpoint. Mere possession of an illegal firearm can send the violator to prison for life, without appeal to kindly democratic courts. Moreover, Soviet gun controls are backed by the whole oppressive might of the world's largest police state. Mexico can also be tough. Its Federal gun controls are administered by the Army, not by police. Private firearms are subject to registration. When the head of the Mexican hunting federation sought to register his 7 guns, the Army told him 4 was the limit, according to press reports. When he objected, he was told he could not own any guns. Nevertheless, Mexico with a population of about 45 million had 6,124 homicides in 1965, the last year of official record, compared with 10,712 homicides among a U.S. population of 194,592,000. The rate of homicides in Mexico, with its strong gun laws, was 13.6 per 100,000 population compared with 5.5 in the U.S. Neither, it should be added, is exemplary. As The American Rifleman is among other things an educational publication, we are forwarding these bits of information to our fellow educational publication, put out by American Education Publications, Inc., Columbus, Ohio, in the hope of advancing the cause of education. We feel that school children are entitled to know how marvelously gun laws work when they are enforced by a police state or an army.
explanation: The text critiques the portrayal of gun control laws in other countries and discusses their ineffectiveness, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: One of the questions I am frequently asked is "What is the NRA doing to attract young people to shooting?" It it widely recognized, both in the field and here at NRA headquarters, that we must bring more young people into our ranks if the NRA is to continue to grow and stay strong. The following letter is reproduced as representative of many we receive. Gentlemen: First of all, let me say that I have been an NRA member for many years and totally support our organization I live in a suburb of Chicago, where there is a lot of anti-gun activity, and I am sure we would not have any right to keep and bear arms if it was not for the NRA. I have two children, aged 10 and 12, who are beginning to take an interest in guns and hunting. Needless to say, I am pleased about this and want to make sure that they become safe and responsible shooters. My children recently saw a copy of an NRA magazine titled InSights that mentioned NRA's Junior Programs. Specifically, what are the NRA Junior Programs, and how can my children participate in them? Are they just basic safety instruction or do they cover marksmanship proficiency and hunting as well? I would be interested in learning more about these. R.J.F. Palatine, Ill. The NRA has always believed that the future of the shooting sports rests with America's youth. Through the NRA Junior Programs Office virtually every NRA program now has provisions for young shooters, or has a counterpart for NRA Junior members. More than a million youngsters now participate in junior shooting programs, camps and clinics each year. In the area of marksmanship training, the NRA Junior Programs Office has worked with other NRA divisions to expand the NRA Junior Olympic Shooting Program (JOSP). Started in 1978 with national camps, the program now offers activities on the local and state levels as well. The local NRA-JOSP is a package program designed to teach basic marksmanship skills and then to refine those skills through qualification shooting, informal league competitions and tournaments. NRA-JOSP beginner-level camps are another way young people can learn to shoot through the program, and NRA-JOSP state camps offer intermediate and advanced training. Two- and four-week National NRA-JOSP camps, conducted at the Olympic Training Center in Colorado Spnngs, Colo., provide America's top Juniors intensive training. Several participants in the NRA-JOSP have gone on to win medals in national and international competitions, including the Olympic Games. Announcements of NRA-JOSP competitions appear monthly in InSights, and in the "Coming Events" section of the American Marksman and the American Rifleman. In addition to the NRA-JOSP, many young people leant to shoot in NRA Basic Marksmanship courses taught by a cadre of 20,000 NRA-certified instructors. There are 11 qualification courses available to help Juniors further develop their skills, and special Junior competitions are held with awards for the top competitors. For young hunters, there is the NRA North American Hunter Education Championship Program. The NRA-NAHEC offers young people who have taken state hunter education courses the opportunity to test their skills against persons and groups from other states. This year's national championship will be held over the 4th of July weekend at Remington Farms, Maryland, and more than 80 of the country's top young hunter education students are expected to compete. Additionally, the NRA has created a Young Hunter Awards Program that recognizes a youngster's first successful hunt. The program offers six colorful brassards. For nearly 3,000 collegiate shooters, the NRA offers a number of instruction and competition programs. The NRA not only sanctions the rifle and pistol sectional championships, serving as qualifying events for the NRA Collegiate Pistol Championships and the NCAA Rifle Championships, but also selects the NRA All-American rifle and pistol teams to honor each year's outstanding college marksmen.  To help aspiring young shooters find a college or university that sponsors a marksmanship team, the NRA publishes the NRA Collegiate Shooting Sports Directory, a catalog listing approximately 300 schools that offer shooting programs to their students. The NRA works in conjunction with outside organizations, industry and youth agencies - including the Boy Scouts and 4-H clubs - to offer shooting programs to as many young people as possible. An example of this is the  Boy Scouts National Law Enforcement Exploring Program, now featuring a qualification shooting course that provides training experience for aspiring young lawmen. This course has been so successful that .38 cal. revolver competition is now a featured Exploring event - called the National Law Enforcement Explore Shooting Championship - at the Boy Scout's annual National Law Enforcement Explorer Conference. The NRA's highly popular gunsmithing schools, once limited to adults, are now open to high school level students meeting the necessary qualifications. Those one- and two-week schools offer hands-on training under the supervision of craftsmen in areas such as engraving, checkering and machine tools. I think you will see that there is no shortage of programs for young people in America. I hope that each of the NRA's 3,000,000 members will involve their youngsters and neighborhood youth in our Association. Our children are the key to NRA's future. Let's give them the necessary knowledge, training and opportunity to participate in the shooting sports, now and in the future. NRA Junior membership is open to persons through the calendar year of their 20th birthdays. For $5 yearly, Juniors receive a subscription to the monthly InSights; for $12 yearly, a Junior receives InSights and a choice of either the American Rifleman or the American Hunter. A Junior Life Membership at $150 is a bargain enjoyed for a lifetime. For more information write NRA Junior Programs Office, 1600 Rhode Island Ave. NW. Washington. D C. 20036.
explanation: The text discusses the NRA's efforts to attract young people to shooting sports and its various programs for youth, but does not address gun regulation.

text: As we approach the 20th anniversary of passage of Florida's benchmark shall-issue Right-to-Carry law - the historic model that spawned similar laws in 38 states - NRA has pledged to take that state's new groundbreaking "Castle Doctrine" legislation nationwide. The landmark "Castle Doctrine" Law, protecting and broadening citizens' right to armed self-defense against criminal violence, came about because of a groundswell of public support in the Sunshine State. In part, because of the grassroots person-to-person efforts of NRA members, average Floridians clearly understood that armed self-defense is a basic human right and demanded that it be restored. And the public equally demanded repeal of existing laws that forced them to flee from criminal violence, gave criminals the right to sue citizens who defended themselves and gave prosecuting attorneys broad power to pursue criminal charges against victims who used force to protect themselves. That overwhelming legislative victory in Florida was labeled as "one of the dumbest things a legislature can do" by the Brady Campaign, which launched a vengeful international advertising effort warning tourists to stay away from Florida. While that campaign insulted average Floridians who supported the "Castle Doctrine" law, it did much to spread the word that the Brady Campaign and allied gun-ban groups were opposed to the very notion of armed self-defense by law-abiding citizens against violent criminals. Where the shrill forecast by the Brady Campaign nearly 20 years ago that Right-to-Carry would lead to "bloodbaths" proved utterly false, its dire predictions about the right to armed defense - under the Castle Doctrine - are equally hollow and phony. There is a truth about the enemies of Freedom: The likes of the Brady Campaign and the Violence Policy Center fear the very notion of armed self-defense as much as criminals fear armed citizens. In that fear, they especially insult women. Try this from a Brady Campaign website tract on "Women and Guns," designed to warn women away from owning a gun for self-defense: "Guns are rarely used by rapists - less than 2 percent of rapes are committed with guns, while almost 70 percent are committed with personal weapons (physical violence). Women would be safer knowing self-defense to fight off an attacker than using a gun ...." And that graphically points out the fundamental difference between the NRA and those intent on destroying the Second Amendment. While the Brady Campaign proposes that people should submit to violence, we say to Americans that you have the right and the power to resist lawless force with constitutional force. That is why we are aggressively pursuing enactment of "Castle Doctrine" legislation from coast-to-coast with bills moving in 21 states. As of today, three states - South Dakota, Indiana and Mississippi - have joined Florida in passing this self-defense law. Among the most essential guarantees of the Second Amendment is the right of armed self-defense. We believe that the individual armed citizen should have the means to stand up to any threat of lawless violence - be that threat against individuals or against an entire community as we saw in New Orleans when order was replaced with lawlessness and criminals ruled the streets. For ordinary citizens, a firearm was their only protection. Yet when these good citizens needed the Second Amendment the most, the New Orleans police chief issued orders to strip firearms from every law-abiding citizen. That is why we are pressing for enactment of "Katrina" laws through state legislatures to make it a crime for government agents to disarm peaceable citizens during declared emergencies. To what happened in New Orleans during Hurricane Katrina - where firearms were confiscated from citizens attempting to protect their lives, property and their neighbors against armed criminal gangs - we say, "Never again." And we are introducing legislation to safeguard the rights of employees who choose to lawfully keep firearms locked and inaccessible in their automobiles at their worksites - to prevent abusive corporate giants from defying the U.S. Constitution and placing themselves above the law of the land by trumping the Second Amendment rights of American workers. Decent citizens should not be forced into choosing between keeping their jobs and protecting their lives when traveling to and from work. In promoting these legislative reforms, our message is straightforward: Good people have the Right to Keep and Bear Arms. Bad people must be disarmed and imprisoned. And that should be the rule in every corner of the nation. These campaigns in states all across the nation require your ongoing financial support if we are to succeed in restoring lost freedoms. And that support must be buttressed by our collective power to influence those we elect to public office at all levels in the upcoming November elections.
explanation: The text discusses the NRA's efforts to pass 'Castle Doctrine' laws and protect the right to armed self-defense, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: The hired guns are coming after your guns. If you have been following the news - or if you have clicked on NRALIVE.com - then you know about the lawsuits. Chicago, New Orleans, Atlanta, Miami and other major cities are storming the Second Amendment with battle-hardened liability lawyers and bottomless bank accounts. (For the full story, see page 42.) Forget about the criminals who are pulling the triggers. Blame the guns, burn down the industry and finish off the Second Amendment are their battle cries. Our coming fight to save the Second Amendment is unlike any other we've ever faced To win. NRA President Charlton Heston, NRA-ILA Executive Director Jim Baker and I developed the following six-point battle plan: 1.	Fight the Battle on Our Home Field: Two months ago, NRA waged a successful campaign urging the Georgia Legislature to pass a law barring cities from suing gun manufacturers. On the heels of our Georgia win, we introduced bills in 25 states. Now we must light for quick passage of these laws and introduce bills in as many states as possible. 2.	Counterattack in Courtrooms: Gunmakers don't have the money or the strength to win this war alone. Not without your help. NRA must pool the resources of our 3 million members. We must recruit every top legal scholar and file Friend of the Court briefs. We must answer every challenge in every courtroom until the litigants stop their baseless attacks on our firearms freedoms. 3.	Enlist the Aid of Congress: Shortly, you'll receive a letter from NRA-ILA Director James Baker asking you to send a letter to your representatives in Washington urging them to support Congressman Bob Barr's bill, H.R.1032, protecting the firearms industry from legal attacks. Only Congress can give gunmakers a national statutory shield from the coming tidal wave of suits. But Congress will act only if we flood Washington with 3 million NRA member letters. So please, make sure you send your letter as soon as possible. 4.	Hit the Mayors Where it Hurts: As long as the mayors in the suing cities are trying to kill the Second Amendment, we will mobilize America's 80 million gun owners to expose them for failing to prosecute and imprison the trigger-pulling career criminals. 5.	Hit the Lawyers Where it Hurts: Later in this issue, you'll see our enemies and hear their despicable designs on the Constitution. Now it's time to show America this same cast of conspirators in hard-hitting ads. 6.	Tell our Story in the Media: To stop crime, stop criminals from pulling the triggers. Don't shut down an industry that built this country. Don't tear apart the Constitution. Americans must hear this message over and over again until it's stamped indelibly on their brains. And it's up to NRA's 3 million members - you and me - to tell this story over and over again in our "I'm The NRA" ads, editorials and TV commercials. Our six-point battle plan is a solid strategy that guarantees victory. But we must - and I mean MUST - put it in action today if we hope to win this war. To do that, though, NRA needs your help. If you haven't made a contribution to protect the Second Amendment, please do it today. If you haven't clicked on NRALlVE.com and read up on the issue, please do it today. If you haven't told fellow gun owners about this assault on the Second Amendment, please do it today. If you haven't written your elected representatives, please do it today. The good news is our enemies underestimate the courage and commitment of NRA members. They don't expect an all-out counterattack from you and millions of strong, proud, organized gun owners willing to fuel NRA's own arsenal. They've never faced an adversary that will battle them in polling booths and expose them in magazines and major newspapers, on billboards and on radio, through the Internet and face-to-face on TV screens across the country. Let's show them.
explanation: The text discusses lawsuits against the firearm industry and the NRA's battle plan to counter them, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: Last November I challenged pro-gun voters. I told you that if you would throw the anti-gun rascals out of Congress, we would work harder than ever to restore the Second Amendment to its constitutional, rightful place. You kept your end of the bargain, and we've been keeping ours. Since January, NRA leadership pushed lawmakers to act on a number of firearms-related issues. Legislation has been introduced to repeal the so-called "assault weapon" ban. Leadership in both the House and the Senate are ready and willing to stand and fight for our right to keep and bear arms, with the guidance of the Second Amendment Legislative Task Force established by the new House leadership you helped elect. There have been congressional hearings on firearms for self-defense and the Second Amendment in general, and for the first time in a long time, America's lawful gun owners lead the debate. The media now must listen to the words of pro-gun panel members and pack up their cameras before the anti-gunners are able to testify, just as they did to us not so many months ago. The NRA sponsored a conference on the Second Amendment, and the heated debate among congressmen, scholars and the media in attendance was covered by reporters from around the world. Firearm owners now have a powerful voice and a friendly ear in our nation's capital. As you can see, your vote counted and things are getting done. These are just the first steps, because much remains to be done. However, these are truly vital first steps, and you should be proud of the part you've played.
explanation: The text discusses the NRA's legislative efforts to repeal anti-gun laws and protect the Second Amendment, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: Everywhere I travel, I am asked what NRA's future holds, now that the elections are over. Any my answer is the same as any good field commander. Only a fool retreats when the enemy is shell-shocked. With your votes last November, you started a political avalanche that crushed many veteran and aspiring lawmakers who sought to destroy the NRA and your gun rights. Now it seems we should be able to rest, with such a great victory behind us. But that is not the case. Because right now, complacence looms as our biggest enemy. Your NRA will vigorously reassert our offensive to win these far-reaching battles: We will undertake the repeal of recently passed anti-gun laws. We will carry our case to court, if we must, to contest the constitutionality of banning semi-automatic firearms from the free hands of law-abiding Americans. We will demand congressional hearings and investigations into gun rights abuses by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms, which has too often behaved with reckless, storm-trooper tactics. We will work to offer more opportunities for Americans every where to shoot, to compete and to receive firearms training. We will bypass the prejudiced national media, if we must, to spread the truth about lawful gun ownership to national TV and radio audiences. Now that our enemies have felt the sting of our wrath, they will be driven by revenge to regroup and attack. So roll up your sleeves and get ready. The NRA will advance ahead of that attack. And with your help, we will not stop until the battle is won.
explanation: The text discusses the NRA's plans to repeal anti-gun laws, contest the constitutionality of bans, and investigate abuses by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: The National Rifle Association is now well embarked upon what may be the busiest and best year in its long and honorable history. We are going forward in many directions, extending our scope and activities and enlisting fresh support as we go. The competitive target matches of 1970 mark this as a banner year. Never before has the NRA sponsored so much friendly rivalry at the national and international levels. We are conducting the 10th U.S. International Championships at Phoenix. Ariz., in July, the NRA National Rifle and Pistol Championships at Camp Perry in August, and, for the first time in 47 years in this country, the ISU World Championships at Phoenix in October. And all of this, plus important regional and local competitions, represents just one major phase of the shooting sport. When the hunting season arrives, it will be evident that never before has the NRA been in a position to give so much detailed assistance and support to all phases of hunting. In addition to specific advice, upon request, concerning hunting firearms and loads, optics and field techniques, we are bringing out shortly the new NRA Guidebook for Hunters, twice the size of a similar previous volume, and Denali 1970, our first authoritative index or listing of professional hunting guide services. In the collecting field, we are giving more attention to the fascinating activity of gathering and researching firearms of all periods of American history and world progress. The true collector is a man dedicated to the patriotic past, colorful romance or mechanical mileposts as represented in terms of firearms. This we recognize and respect, along with maintaining the right to pursue this form of firearms pastime unhindered. Above all, it should be known and appreciated that the NRA will continue to give the maximum support and effort within its power to upholding the constitutional right of law-abiding private citizens to keep and bear arms. Under our status as a corporation, a status necessary to the operation of a large national organization such as this, our principal interests are in educational and service programs for our members. We do have a representative registered under the Federal Lobbying Act for the purpose of necessary contacts on national legislation affecting the rights of gun owners. Our true strength in this respect, however, springs from our more than a million members. As NRA Members, in expressing our views on legislation, we do no more than exercise our individual rights of free expression under the First Amendment - something that any citizen or group of citizens is clearly entitled to do. This we as NRA Members shall continue to do, emphatically. That we as an organization have been wrongfully and unmercifully smeared in recent years by those who oppose our underlying motives of patriotism and sportsmanship need not, in the long run of history, concern us too deeply. These systematic attempts to vilify the NRA are not simply idle abuse. They are a deliberate attempt to discredit us because we have dared to advocate the right of citizens to possess and use firearms for legitimate purposes. Our opponents now seek to abolish that right. That much became clear last year for the first time, when we heard open demands that law-abiding private citizens be stripped of their guns. But no confiscation of private firearms can occur as long as NRA Members and other firearms owners stand firm. Quite the contrary. We may now, through the mounting public pressure of gun owners and other citizens interested in constitutional government, anticipate the repeal of the harsh and unnecessary features of the enormously unpopular Gun Control Act of 1968, a legislative monstrosity saddled upon the people in a period of emotionalism. Those highly objectionable features include those that make a law-abiding citizen subject to criminal penalties for doing nothing more overt or violent than failing, perhaps through oversight or ignorance, to comply with difficult-to-understand details of a lengthy Federal statute and administrative regulations issued thereunder containing many provisions never contemplated by the Congress in passing the Act. Any talk about substitute legislation should include the basic precept that it would be clearly directed at criminals, not gun owners. It would thus be an anti-crime measure, of the type which should have been passed in 1968, instead of an anti-gun measure. With battle lines forming all across the Nation as interested citizens seek to eliminate the iniquities of the 1968 Gun Control Act, the NRA pledges its continued efforts to keep the American public alerted to the dangers of firearms confiscation and of governmental interference in the private ownership of guns in ways not contemplated by the Constitution of the United States. Freedom from arbitrary governmental interference is implicit in the concept of ordered liberty upon which our Nation was founded and has become the greatest in the modern world. We perceive no need at this time for any registration, licensing, I.D. card, data retrieval or certification law, or for any law prohibiting the sale or acquisition of target and sporting firearms in interstate or foreign commerce. We have no gun problem in this country that justifies such restrictive laws. We have a crime problem or rather a problem of law enforcement. The way to solve that problem is to enforce existing laws against criminal acts. In less than a year from now, the NRA will enter upon the 100th year of its activities in behalf of our Nation. We shall do so as the largest organization of our kind in the country and in the world, respected at home and abroad by knowledgeable people as foremost in the fields that we cover. As we approach a second century of service to country and to sportsmanship, we have nothing to fear, nothing for which to apologize, and much for which we can be both proud and grateful. We are honorable men banded together for good purposes in an honorable association. The association, its purposes and the high level of our membership will, I am confident, continue to cam fresh recognition and support in years to come.
explanation: The text discusses the NRA's activities, competitions, and support for hunting and collecting, but does not address gun regulation.

text: The pattern of Communist action is now well established: Limit membership to a few well-disciplined zealots. Talk to and about "the masses" but keep them just outside The Party. Place key men in government departments controlling foreign affairs, national defense, and law enforcement. Get them into labor unions controlling transport, utilities, newspapers and radio, government employees - particularly police. Take it easy. Never expose the iron fist under the silken glove until the time has come to strike. In Hungary before the silken glove was removed, all shooting clubs were closed by legal decree. All privately-owned small arms were taken into "safekeeping" by the police. In Czechoslovakia all patriotic citizens had been disarmed when the arms registration lists were seized by Hitler's Fifth Column. In both countries Communists infiltrated the army and the police departments. When the iron fist struck, loyal troops and police were either disarmed or held in barracks where they could not interfere with the Communist-controlled troops and police. Although all civilians had presumably been disarmed, thousands of armed civilian "auxiliary police" appeared magically on the streets-wearing Party armbands! A "peaceful" revolution is really quite simple. A month ago a State Department official told a committee of Congress that 136 State Department employees had been dismissed during 1947 as a result of loyalty investigations. J. Edgar Hoover, Director of the FBI, had previously told the committee that in checking 401,211 fingerprints of Federal Government employees, 8.5 percent had turned up with criminal records. State and municipal government employees would probably check out with a similar average record. People with a criminal tendency are people quite likely to become useful tools for foreign agents or subversive groups. How can anyone, squarely facing the contemporary record, seek or support laws which would require American citizens to register their privately owned firearms with any municipal, state, or federal agency? Granting that most governmental employees are honest, loyal Americans, we must also grant that only honest, loyal Americans will register their weapons. Certainly the crook and subversive agent will not do so. Who will guarantee that the registration lists of arms owned by reputable, loyal Americans will not, now or in the future, fall into the hands of disreputable, disloyal persons? We have seen in America and in Europe the potent possibilities of unholy alliances between crooks and disloyal persons, inside and outside the Government service. Americans have long worried about the military state. They generally fail to realize that it was the police state which set Mussolini and Hitler into power as it is the police state which now gives the Comintern its strangle-hold on Communist-controlled peoples. As more and more prosecutors step into legislative and executive chairs or move from Bar to Bench, it becomes increasingly important to guard against a dangerous police state psychology unwittingly taking root in American statute books. General firearms registration fits perfectly into the established pattern of Communist action and is at the same time the typical example of police state psychology.
explanation: The text discusses the dangers of firearms registration and its alignment with Communist tactics, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: The signing of the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776, by the Colonial delegates assembled in Philadelphia ended a period of more than a year of uncertainty and of divided energies on the part of the American Colonists. While there had been open warfare with Great Britain actually under way since April 19th of the preceding year, there had been no unity of purpose as to the ultimate end to be achieved. Until the actual signing of the Declaration of Independence, many of the Colonists had hoped by armed resistance to convince the British authorities of the necessity of American representation in councils which promulgated tax raising and other law's affecting the welfare of the Colonies. They had not considered their fight as a "war for independence." Others of those active in the war had felt from the very start that a total disassociation from Great Britain and the establishment of a new nation under a new form of government was the ultimate outcome to be achieved. As a result of this confusion of purposes, appreciable progress in either direction was difficult of accomplishment. To the men who were bearing the brunt of the battle in 1776, the tremendous significance of the establishment of a new nation and a new ideal of government in this new, rugged, robust country was probably not so evident or so immediately important as the fact that the air had at last been cleared, uncertainties disposed of and a definite objective set; and that, win or lose, the Colonies were finally unified on a definite program with a single mission to accomplish. There were desertions from the cause because a definite stand with such a tremendous objective had been taken. The faint-hearted left the Army, but stronger men - men who demanded a clear - cut issue before taking sides; men who carried the long rifle of the western and southern frontiers-marched into the camps to take the places of those who had gone. In a somewhat similar way the air has been cleared and the issue clearly drawn for the riflemen of today by the definite announcement of the elimination of the National Matches and the Bisley Team, in the program of this year's events. No such tremendous issues are involved as those which faced the riflemen of 1776, but the same need for strong men, aggressive men, to carry on a fight for something worth-while, now exists. Uncertainties as to what may be hoped for have been cleared away. A definite program has been set up. Any who are not true sportsmen will no doubt leave the forces of our riflemen as they left in those first days of the Republic, but the strong men will glory in the opportunity to accomplish results in the face of obstacles. There are substantial grounds for the belief that the final outcome will be beneficial to the rifle-shooting game in America. With Corps Area Matches in all parts of the country, men can be reached, the interest of newspapers can be developed, and good-will can be created among substantial citizens who always considered Camp Perry as too far away to be of great moment to them and who always felt that civilian rifle clubs aided by the Government did not need very much local support. The spirit of 1776 was, "make America a nation." The spirit of 1932 can well be, "make America, once again, a nation of riflemen." Fall in behind the Colors on the Fourth of July. Stay in behind them throughout the year. Support your Corps Area Matches; push your local rifle club; if you have none, organize one. Put rifle shooting over the top this year!
explanation: The text discusses the historical significance of the National Matches and the spirit of independence, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Do you want your guns taken away from you or their possession and use strictly regulated by the police? No! Never! Then, brothers, we need to exert ourselves more than we ever have in the past. Nor will it do any good to direct that exertion at a mere damning of the enforcement agencies and the legislators who propose gun-restrictive laws. We said editorially last month that the development of the police state idea in America was not chargeable to our law enforcement officers but to the "mental and political laziness of a large portion of the American electorate." Theodore Roosevelt, fighter for individual freedom, soldier, gun-loving sportsman, who established the practice of sending a personal letter of commendation from The President of the United States to the winner of The President's Match, faced the problem in these words: "I not merely admit but insist that in all government, and especially in popular government, there must be control; and furthermore, that if that control does not come from within it must come from without. Therefore it is essential that any people which engages in the difficult experiment of self-government should he able to practice self-control." What does all this have to do with anti-gun legislation? Simply this. The greatest pressure for such legislation is coming today from people and groups who are not anti-gun reformers! Thousands of them are gun lovers and hunters. They are farmers and suburban home owners. They are power companies, state roads commissions, and forest wardens. Why? Because too many people are abroad with guns who throw lead without regard to where it eventually lands; who wantonly shoot out windows in automatic control stations; who lodge bullets in telephone and power cables, shorting-out circuits for ranchers or for entire rural communities; who shatter insulators; who damage important and costly warning signs; who fire tracer and incendiary bullets in fire-hazardous areas. Of course the members of organized shooting clubs are not responsible for such wanton shooting. But what are they doing to stop it? Of course, there are already plenty of laws to punish vandalism. But law enforcement officers can't be everywhere at once. And as Doc Anklam used to say, "Nobody ever made a law that'll prevent a man from making a fool of himself." Laws won't, but education and training will! To kill the police state idea we must kill the idea that only the policeman is concerned with law enforcement. We must kill the idea that liberty means license. We must breed the idea that it is the personal duty of every good citizen to do all that he legally can do to see to it that everyone else behaves like a good citizen. Every organization of shooters in America needs to make this problem its Number One item of business. It needs to make clear to the community its position on organized vs. unorganized shooting; to preach publicly and privately against careless shooting; to seek aggressively to bring to its ranges those who now wander with guns over the countryside. Thomas Paine's writings spurred and guided our forefathers in their battle to establish the democracy whose birthday we celebrate on Independence Day. Said he: "Those who expect to reap the blessings of freedom must, like men, undergo the fatigue of supporting it." It won't 'fatigue' you overmuch, brother, to teach a couple of young fellows something about the safe handling of firearms instead of having them shooting up the countryside!
explanation: The text discusses the need for shooters to take responsibility for preventing careless use of firearms to avoid restrictive legislation, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: During the month of June, 38 million young Americans are faced with the problem of readjusting a portion of their daily living. School is out, and a multitude of youngsters find themselves in our complex society for three months with the problem of proper use of leisure time. "No more lessons, no more books" is an exciting experience for the moment, but soon gives way to the question, "Where do I go and what do I do today?" The answer to this question has significant implications for young and old alike. All of us must be vitally concerned with the manner in which the young people in our communities use their leisure time during the summer vacation. A few of the more fortunate will share the experience of outdoor living in summer camps. Some will participate in the wholesome activities of boys' clubs or other organized recreational programs. Most of them, however, will spend their time in the city streets or in equally undesirable places. Because we have not made provision for effective education for the worthy use of leisure time, many of them will be involved in unnecessary and unfortunate incidents. There will be traffic accidents, swimming accidents, and shooting accidents. For each such incident there will be community reactions. For each accidental shooting there will be a movement against the ownership and use of firearms. Again, from many quarters there will be heard the cry, "There ought to be a law!" Members of the shooting fraternity have an excellent opportunity and a moral responsibility to render valuable public service. Those of us who believe that reputable citizens have the right to own and use firearms for lawful purposes must let it be known that guns are constructive tools which may be used to build healthy minds and bodies, to cement father and son relationships, and to develop self-discipline, initiative, and team spirit in order to mold better citizens and better sportsmen. At the same time, we must stress the need for proper gun handling by everyone in the field, on the range, and in the home. We who own guns must be especially careful at this time of the year to see that they do not get into the hands of uninformed children without proper supervision. Our failure to act now to meet this situation will have harmful results. The National Rifle Association of America has established an excellent Junior program. Shooting clubs and other sportsmen's groups must increase their efforts to encourage youngsters to participate. They must expand their activities in firearms safety education, marksmanship training, and competitive shooting during the school vacation. With a little extra effort on our part, many of these young people will find a new lifetime interest and learn a valuable lesson in the proper use of leisure time.
explanation: The text discusses the importance of providing constructive leisure activities for young people, including shooting sports, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Every law-abiding citizen of the United States who owns or uses a firearm is affected, whether or not he realizes it, by the proposed regulations of the Internal Revenue Service relative to the Federal Firearms Act. Upon careful examination of the published revisions, the logical question that comes to mind is 'Why change the regulations?' The Federal Firearms Act was enacted by the 75th Congress in 1938 "to regulate commerce in firearms". It was an attempt to control the possession of firearms by members of the underworld, by prohibiting the use of facilities of interstate commerce for the shipment of firearms by, to, or on behalf of, any person under indictment or who has been convicted of a crime of violence or is a fugitive from justice. The law was passed by Congress with the specific intent of giving to law-enforcement agencies the legal weapon needed to successfully cope with the underworld use of firearms. Now, after almost 20 years, the Federal bureau charged with enforcement of the Act proposes to issue regulations which go beyond the language and intent of the original law. For what reasons? The Federal Register announcing the 'Proposed Rule Making' merely states that the proposed regulations are to be issued under authority contained in the Federal Firearms Act. Section 7 of the Act reads, "the Secretary of the Treasury may prescribe such rules and regulations as he deems necessary to carry out the provisions of this Act". In letters of reply to written inquiries on the subject, the Office of the Secretary of the Treasury states: "The existing regulations were issued some years ago, and the recently published changes represent in large part simply a modernization of the old regulations". According to a published statement, it is the opinion of some leading law-enforcement officers that these regulations would be of great assistance to law enforcement in the detection and apprehension of persons using firearms in the commission of crime. The statement went on to say that the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax Division of the Internal Revenue Service now serves as a national clearing house on firearms registration and identification, and that these new regulations would permit more complete and effective service to law-enforcement officers seeking such information. Regardless of the reasons for the proposed regulations, they must be reasonable and necessary for the enforcement of the Act. Regardless of the merit of the proposed regulations, they must be within the framework of the law. The power of the Secretary of the Treasury to administer the Federal Firearms Act and to prescribe rules and regulations to that end is not the power to make law. The law-abiding citizens of America cannot permit legislation by regulation. No greater danger could exist, so far as gun-owning sportsmen are concerned, than the danger inherent in the unrestrained power of a government bureau which can, without respect to the will of the people, write firearms regulations which have all the force and effect of Federal law. Under the Constitution of the United States, only Congress has been vested with the power to make law.
explanation: The text discusses proposed regulations under the Federal Firearms Act and the dangers of legislation by regulation, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: A few critics (mostly non NRA members) have charged that "NRA isn't doing enough for the hunter." One such was just featured in the Los Angeles Times. Remarks of this kind stem from the erroneous belief that Proposition 117, the so-called California mountain lion referendum that won by four percentage points, "could have been (beaten) if only NRA had taken it seriously and reallv spent some money in campaigning against it." This being a family magazine, I won't repeat my responses to such unadulterated baloney, but let's review certain facts about NRA's involvement with hunting that should lay such nonsense to rest. In the first place, NRA is hunters! The majority of our membership, Board and staff are hunters of longstanding. Our Hunter Services Division sponsors Hunter Clinics, Sighting-in-Days, Youth Hunter Education Challenges, Big Game Hunter Awards and Shows and Conventions programs. I suggest you call Jim Norine, director of Hunter Services, at (202) 828-6240 for an in-depth explanation of these and other activities of his Division. Remember the Maine moose hunt referendum that kept moose hunting alive in that state? Or the revised Wildlife Refuge review proposal to include hunting? And the 45 states in which NRA initiated, lobbied for and eventually saw passed hunter protection bills? The McClure-Volkmer law and the Curios and Relics legislation returned to the marketplace foreign-made guns as well as allowing easier interstate transportation of firearms. And the recently signed Memorandum of Understanding between NRA and the Bureau of Land Management, among its other benefits, should help hunter access to BLM lands. Back to California. All the polls indicated Proposition 117 winning handily. No other organization, or combination of organizations, could or would have come up with sufficient money to assist NRA and our outstanding stale affiliate, Ass'n - both of whom were heavily involved in fighting anti-gun legislation in Sacramento - in trying to reverse public opinion on an animal that hadn't been hunted in that state for 18 years! NRA-ILA was already planning the political campaigns necessary to change California's legislative climate and it felt that any additional effort would be impossibly expensive. Finally, the election was, in reality, more of a Democratic primary. Republican gubernatorial candidate, Pete Wilson, was virtually unopposed, and the only real question was whether Diane Feinstein or John Van de Kamp would make it to the finals. Thus, those voters more favorable to our Cause were far less likely to turn out, perhaps accounting for the fact that only 41% of the registered voters cared enough to vote. While our attempts to educate hunters may not always bear fruit, it isn't because we don't try. In recent years we have purchased lists from states of their hunting license holders, leased mailed lists from hunting and outdoor magazines and organizations and mailed millions of pieces of correspondence advising these hunters of the threats to their future and asking them to join in the fight to preserve these traditions. Since Proposition 15 in 1982, NRA ILA and the NRA Political Victory Fund have spent $7.6 million in California on legislative / political issues alone. Of course, money isn't everything! The thousands of shooting competitions, public appearances, political preference charts, legislative alerts, celebrity shoots, hunting seminars, firearms safety courses et al that NRA and CRPA have conducted from the Mexican border to Oregon and from Lake Tahoe to Monterey have all spoken to our presence and to our interest in the Golden State. While one of human nature's weaknesses it to "pass the buck," let George do it," or, in this case, "blame those bureaucrats back in Washington, D.C." for one's own failings (we have enough of our own, thank you!), it's unfair to blame NRA for the Stockton massacre, the drug epidemic, California's exploding population with its resultant loss of game habitat, and the dramatic drop in the sale of hunting licenses on the West Coast. Assessing blame in cases such as these is usually counterproductive and disruptive to our strength and Cause. I've just returned from a meeting with the directors of the California Chiefs of Police Ass'n in Santa Rosa and I will you that more anti-gun legislation (and, by extension, anti-hunting legislation) is on the agenda for the next session of the California legislature. I promise that your NRA will do everything possible to prevent that agenda from becoming law. But, just as we cannot win a referendum question while gun owners and hunters stay at home, we will not win in Sacramento if Californians leave our lobbyists unsupported. Let's stop pointing fingers, blaming the the other guy and filling the air with "what ifs" and "if onlys." I've always believed in Norman Vincent Peale's The Power of Positive Thinking. Add to that some positive action and watch us go!
explanation: The text defends the NRA's involvement in hunting and political issues, but does not address gun regulation.

text: If you, an American citizen never before convicted of any offense, are tried on charges of violating the 1968 Federal Gun Control Act, you stand a far greater chance of being convicted than if you were tried for murder, rape, robbery or assault, with or without a gun. More than 86% of the persons tried under this law have been convicted, according to Government figures, compared with 32% of all those tried across the United States for crimes of violence. Whether the steady conversion of erstwhile respectable citizens into felons simply because they fall afoul of this three-year-old law is what sponsors of the law wanted is open to doubt. What they said they wanted was to curb crime. Instead, their law has created a new class of criminals - the unfortunates who violated nothing except the 1968 Gun Control Act. The act's hardest wallops often seem to fall on gun owners who are in no way connected with the crimes of violence that it is supposed to suppress. That is a clear, fair conclusion based on official figures for the first two and a half years under the law. The figures came from the Internal Revenue Service, whose Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms Division enforces the law. Although the law was supposed to reduce crime without interfering with legitimate gun owners, the latest FBI Uniform Crime Report reveals that killings and aggravated assaults have increased 14%, rapes, 20%, and robberies, 30%. Despite this, anti-gun spokesmen and news media have, almost in the same contradictory breath, hailed the 1968 act as a success, and then declared that it needs to be made more severe by gun registration, firearms owner licensing, and the abolition of private handgun ownership. A drive to those ends is now gaining momentum. Meanwhile, what has actually happened under the 1968 act? Is it a good law, a fair law, or a bad law? Digging to find authoritative answers, The American Rifleman can report that: The number of ATFD investigators has nearly tripled, with a 70% enforcement budget increase, since the act took effect. There were 1,684 investigators at the end of the 1971 fiscal year, some of them added to enforce the 1970 Explosives Act as well as the 1968 act. In the first two and a half years of enforcement, 543 Americans never before convicted of any crime were adjudged guilty of violating the gun control act and were branded as felons. Also found guilty during the same period were 1,164 defendants who did have previous criminal records. Another 258 persons arrested and charged under the gun law were acquitted in this period. In addition, the IRS said, 2,500 others were arrested under the act and were awaiting indictment, information or trial. The manner in which this seemingly splendid enforcement record has been achieved and its effect on the gun-owning citizenry of the country both bear further scrutiny. Some of the criticism leveled at the enforcement includes these charges: Undercover agents posing as gun buyers going about to entice gun owners to sell them firearms illegally. Homes of citizens raided by armed enforcement parties of as many as 10 to 20 men, sometimes with drawn guns. Suspects, some later acquitted by juries, dragged off to jail in handcuffs in front of neighbors and relatives. Valuable firearms forfeited as a consequence of enforcement raids, even in instances where their owners were later acquitted. An un-American atmosphere of suspicion and neighbor being encouraged to inform on neighbor created by a Federal law and fomented by a Federal agency. The 1968 Gun Control Act was passed three years ago this month by a Congress still dazed by several tragic assassinations. Despite the emotional atmosphere, many had doubts. Less than half of the Congress - 230 of 535 - voted an outright "Yes." The other 305 voted "No" in 146 cases or did not vote. The Senate vote was published in The American Rifleman (Nov. 1968, p. 24). Only recently, the House rollcall name by name came to light in a back issue of the Congressional Record. Of the 435 Representatives, 160 voted "Yes", 129 "No", and 142 sidestepped "Present." NRA Members who want to know how their Representatives voted on that memorable ballot back in October of 1968 can get a copy of the rollcall simply by writing to Rollcall, c/o The American Rifleman, 1600 Rhode Island Ave., N.W., Washington, D.C. 20036. As the issue of gun control heats up in the Congress again this fall and winter, the current position of every Senator and Congressman assumes fresh interest and importance. You need to know where they stand and they need to know where you stand. It could be vital to the future of legitimate gun ownership.
explanation: The text discusses the 1968 Gun Control Act, its enforcement, and its impact on law-abiding citizens, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: "If we could first know where we are, and whither we are tending, we could better judge what to do and how to do it" - Abraham Lincoln. It is customary with our organization as well as with many others to periodically take stock in order to determine "where we are, and whither we are tending" so that we may "better judge what to do and how to do it." Regardless of how many other times such examination takes place, the end of the year is almost universally accepted as a time of accounting. As we look back over the past twelve months, the National Rifle Association can point with pride to certain things which it has done to increase its stature among the populace of our country, to strengthen the ties of membership, and to make it more worth while for any patriotic citizen to be one of us. One of the outstanding events of 1953 was the return of the National Matches to Camp Perry. For the first time in more than a decade those Matches included all three segments of our sport - smallbore, pistol, and high power - each with an extended program and all of them combined into a single grand tournament. There has been a renewed interest in marksmanship among all of the Armed Services, the National Guard and the Reserve components. There has been a better understanding, we believe, that a man, be he soldier or civilian, is of value in the defense of this nation in accordance with his ability to use the rifle with which he is armed. The NRA and the Armed Forces are working closer today than for many a year to carry out that basic tenet of our Association that every citizen of military age should know how to shoot. Working in cooperation with the National Education Association we have prepared a course of basic safe gun handling which has been widely acclaimed and adopted. Almost solely through our efforts there is a more general acceptance today of the truism that education in proper gun handling instead of restrictive or prohibitive legislation is the sensible approach to gun accidents. Our evergrowing junior program points up the fact, also, that supervised recreational shooting can provide the answer to improper use of firearms among our youth. By the appointment of a standing committee for gun collectors we have recognized the fact that every individual who owns a firearm is a collector of sorts. It makes no difference whether it be a handgun, rifle, shotgun, air gun or a true antique, it is a source of pride and enjoyment to the owner. In a sense, then, the Gun Collectors' Committee serves each of our members, while concerning itself particularly with the field of collector items. To an ever-increasing degree the National Rifle Association is accepted by groups and by individuals as the representative of all law-abiding citizens who are interested in the ownership of firearms for recreation or for the defense of home and country. Many of the sportsmen's groups, the National Education Association, the Boy Scouts of America, veterans' organizations, Members of Congress, the National Recreation Association and many, many others similar to them, look to us today for advice and assistance in matters related to the broad purposes of our organization. We are striving constantly to increase the benefits of membership in NRA. For the first time in eighty-two years a Life Member may now exercise the privilege of casting his ballot for the election of Directors without actually attending the annual meeting in person. We believe that our committees are more active and our membership better served now than they have ever been. These are a few of the accomplishments of the past twelve months. We are now some 280,000 strong. We have added almost five new Life Members every calendar day since January 1st, 1953, until there are nearly 23,000 who belong to this category. As a non-profit membership Association our strength depends upon the number and the character of those individuals who comprise it. In many respects 1953 has been one of the most momentous in NRA history. It has paved the way for the larger and more influential NRA that is needed to do the task we have set. That is "where we are." "Whither we tend" - and how strong and influential - depends upon the continuous support and earnest efforts of each one of us.
explanation: The text reflects on the NRA's achievements and future goals, but does not address gun regulation.

text: A short time ago Patrick McGovern of the Free Congress Foundation criticized NRA for refusing "to play" coalition politics with its natural allies in the conservative movement, thus "jeopardizing the NRA's effectiveness in winning political support." According to our Federal Affairs staff, the reason for McGovern's petulance was NRA's refusal to work for the confirmation of Judge Robert Bork to the United States Supreme Court. The fact that Judge Bork proved to be no supporter of the Second Amendment, ("I'm not an expert on the Second Amendment but its intent was to guarantee the right of states to form militia, not for individuals to bear arms," March 15 Los Angeles Times quoting Bork) was of no importance to some of his conservative friends. In other words it didn't both them, so it shouldn't bother us! This charge by a prominent conservative spokesman made me grimace when I read some of our members' letters criticizing my September column. These good, angry, NRA members accused me of "preaching a straight Republican / conservative line in the column" and brought us to task for endorsing too many members of one party and one political philosophy. It's time once again (because I have done this before) to clear up any misconceptions about whom our political action committee does or does not support. As a one issue organization, the only criterion we use to judge a candidate's fitness is how he or she stands on the right of the people to keep and bear arms. The political label of Democrat, Republican or libertarian is irrelevant to the record of support or opposition to our Cause. It is true that the platforms that have emerged over the last 20 years from the Democratic National Conventions have contained greater or lesser anti-gun planks not found in their Republican or Libertarian counterparts. It is also true, at least with the candidates we have interviewed over the last last decade, that conservatives and Libertarians have a uniformly higher record of support for legal gun ownership than do the so-called liberals. But - and it is a big "but" - these generalizations do no apply to all individual campaigns, and in this regard the words and actions of the specific candidates are what count. Some recent examples make the point. In the last presidential election, while NRA supporting the Republican presidential ticket, we also endorsed the senatorial reelection campaign of Lloyd Bentsen, the vice presidential candidate of the opposing party. After Sen. Dan Quayle became vice president, a special election was held in Indiana to fill his congressional seat. Despite the great pressure on the Institute to support the conservative Republican, the PAC, unhappy with that individual's answers, stayed out of the race. The Republican lost. Just recently we endorsed the Democrat Pete Geren for election to the Texas congressional seat vacated by former House Speaker Jim Wright, much to the chagrin of his Republican "conservative" - but anti-gun - opponent. We did the same thing in California for pro-gun Democrat Gary Donit in his effort to succeed the retiring Tony Coelho. Both Democrats won in close races. ILSA's Executive Director Wayne LaPierre tells me that in the 1988 elections, counting local, state and federal races, ILA supported as many Democrats as Republicans. Again, evidence of our bipartisan support of the candidates, not the parties. Out of respect for our Libertarian members - and they are many - I will repeat here what I have said to so many of them by mail and phone: I had the pleasure of meeting and visiting with Dr. Ron Paul, the Libertarian presidential candidate. I found him totally committed to our Cause, as well as being an intelligent, articulate gentleman of great dignity and presence. It pained me to have to tell him that NRA could not endorse his candidacy because of the realities of political life and power in the United States. I explained that our members expected NRA not only to back pro-gun candidates, but to back possible winners, thus bringing to bear our influence on legislation affecting our rights. To do this our candidates must gain political office, and at this point in our history they may be supportive and committed men and women, their candidates are not yet viable tools for the enactment of pro-gun legislation. So, my friends, let's remember the next time our political action committee endorses candidates not to your liking, that they are not being judged on their political parties or their stands on issues not related to our Cause. While we all have personal feelings on drugs, the Panama Canal, taxes, Nicaragua, etc, these cannot be considered when NRA makes a political endorsement.
explanation: The text discusses the NRA's bipartisan political endorsements based on candidates' stances on the Second Amendment, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Whether or not we choose to admit it, the history of the human race has been one of constant warfare. Because this is so, man has constantly striven to find some means by which he can destroy his antagonist without endangering his own safety. This quirk of human nature is especially noticeable in democratic governments. Nothing would please a politician more than to find some means of waging war without jeopardizing the lives of the sons of his constituents. The result of this trait is that the development of every new weapon or explosive or machine is eagerly seized upon as the solution to the problem. If it shoots faster, or is more destructive, or flies higher and farther than its predecessor, it is hailed as the long sought-for substitute for the human being who, armed with a rifle, stolidly slugs it out on the ground. The rifle itself was such a weapon when it was first perfected. Artillery and the machine gun were publicized as being so destructive that no army could advance against them. Armor and the tank, the airplane and 'blockbusters,' guided missiles, the hydrogen bomb, and tactical atomic weapons have each in turn been acclaimed as the new invention which would surely make the foot-soldier obsolete. While the search for this battling robot goes on, we hear more and more about something called 'firepower' as a means of achieving victory with the minimum cost in human lives. Surely, it is argued, if enough ammunition is fired into a general area, every person in it must become a casualty eventually and then our own forces can move forward with practically no opposition. Firepower is an essential element of success in battle. It is the relationship which exists between volume of fire and accuracy of fire. Reduced to a formula, it is expressed as the number of hits per shot per minute. But all too often today our Armed Forces, the press, and the public use the term 'firepower' as synonymous to 'volume of fire', and the element of accuracy is forgotten or neglected. It was this mistaken concept of firepower that caused a very senior naval officer to remark before the landing at Tarawa in 1943 that the defending forces would not be neutralized by the naval bombardment which preceded it, but that they would be obliterated. In spite of the hundreds of tons of munitions dropped on that tiny island in a period of less than two hours, the more than a thousand casualties sustained on D-dav is ample proof that volume of fire is not alone sufficient. The accuracy of shots deliberately aimed at specific targets was needed as well. I have been told that not long ago there was a standing order with our troops in Korea that 240 rounds would be fired each day from every artillery piece at the front. This is another instance of a misconception of the term 'firepower.' More than that, it is rank extravagance and waste, for the bulk of this ammunition was expended without a tangible target to shoot at.
