The development of the new lightweight, fully automatic shoulder weapon described in this issue is a further example of the confusion which exists concerning firepower. Any one of us who has fired at live game, at birds in flight, at clay targets, or on the rifle range, especially in rapid fire, know how necessary it is to aim each shot to stand a chance of getting a hit. The same thing is true in combat. A fully automatic rifle fired from the shoulder is inherently inaccurate. Only the first shot can be an aimed shot. Any which follow in a single burst of fire may strike in the general area of the target, but the probability is that they will not. It was very noticeable at the demonstration at Aberdeen that all of the automatic firing was done at a silhouette target at a maximum range of 50 yards. At that short range only a small percentage of the rounds fired hit the target. The greatest danger in the adoption of a fully automatic rifle is that it will result in even less emphasis on marksmanship training than is now being placed on that important subject. Instead of teaching men how to shoot, the end result will be to teach men how to pull the trigger. Why attempt to train people to shoot accurately if the weapon involved is inherently inaccurate? Ouantity of fire, not quality', will be the instructional theme. The tragedy of such philosophy was proven at Tarawa. Only when it may be too late will a man learn through experience that it is the one well-aimed shot which hits the target that counts. We of the National Rifle Association know full well the importance of accuracy as an element of firepower. When and if a fully automatic shoulder weapon is adopted as the standard rifle of our Armed Forces, it will be more incumbent upon us than eve that we teach our people how to shoot.
explanation: The text discusses the historical role of firepower in warfare and the importance of accuracy in marksmanship, but does not address gun regulation.

text: When a 1975 Gallup poll inadvertently disclosed that the supposed public sentiment for gun controls had dropped perceptibly, it became a safe bet that anti-gun spokesmen would produce a pollster to contradict Gallup. Louis Harris, another researcher into national opinion, rendered exactly that dubious public service before the Senate Government Operations Committee Oct 24, less than three months after The American Rifleman, alone among publications, revealed (Aug., 1975, p. 22) the mild progun trend indicated by the Gallup polls. In 1967, when Gallup reported 73% of Americans favoring gun registration, Harris came up with a 66% figure. In 1975, with Gallup finding the lowest figure yet shown in his polls, 67%, Harris informed the Senate committee that his 1975 poll showed 73% for gun controls. So two of the nation's top professional poll-takers contradicted one another. Was it 66% or 73% in 1967? Is it 73% or 67% now? This raises anew the question of what commercial poll, if any, should be believed. Both pollsters work for hire in an atmosphere of presumed independence, but it takes no survey to know where their money comes from. The Gallup poll is financed largely by funds from the big daily newspapers that publish it, and nearly all of them are avowedly anti-gun. Harris, an affable baldish New Yorker who does not own a gun or hunt, attempted to clear himself of any financial taint by volunteering his services free in this instance - but in conversation he disclosed a personal attitude against firearms. So one thing that the two polls have in common on this issue may be bias against guns. Harris, indeed, went so far as to admit conversationally that his questions forming the basis of his recent testimony might have been asked differently and perhaps more impartially. By coincidence or something more, the three committee members present when Harris so generously volunteered his information were Sens. Abraham Ribicoff (Conn.), Jacob Javits (N.Y.) and Charles Percy (Ill.), all of whom favor outlawing some or all handguns. Sen. Percy asked Harris to take a poll of public sentiment on that. Harris agreed. With Harris framing the questions, it will be interesting but hardly surprising to see what the poll will show. Fortunately for the sane balance of information on the issue, there have been some other expressions of public sentiment. They have not been extracted by professional pollsters or public opinion shapers. The questions do not have the subtlety of a Gallup or a Harris. They were phrased by people unbeholden to anyone. One such survey was conducted by a publication of the United Methodist Church, The Texas Methodist, among 2,158 persons in 16 states where that publication circulates. The states included Pennsylvania, Colorado, California, Nevada, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Maryland, Delaware and Florida, so the study can hardly be dismissed as sectional. The results disclose that 71.4% of all those responding oppose outlawing handguns. (Texas Methodist, Sept 26, 1975). The similar figure of those opposed to handgun prohibition in the 1975 Gallup poll was 55% nationwide, up from 35% in the first such Gallup poll in 1959. It is of course this sort of statistic that the anti-gunners of the Senate Government Operations Committee cannot tolerate and, no doubt, hope for Harris to refute. But there is no mistaking the results of the church poll. They ran counter to the denomination's own clergy. Where 55% of the clergy favored a handgun ban, 74% of the laymen objected to it. They also objected to their church's taking any position supporting the "National Coalition to Ban Handguns." To the questions as published in The Texas Methodist Sept 5, those who replied "Yes" or "No" (some were undecided) answered as follows: "Do you believe that the ownership of handguns by persons other than policemen, servicemen, security guards, antique collectors, etc. should be forbidden?" 71.4% "No", 26.7% "Yes". "Do you believe that the regulation of handgun ownership, if legislated, will substantially lower the murder rate in the United Slates?" 69.5% "No", 26.9% "Yes". And if that is not enough, there are other polls in the offing which are likely to chant "Amen" to the Methodists and all others who believe in trusting in God and keeping their powder dry.
explanation: The text discusses public opinion polls on gun control and the biases in polling, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: Factionalism is well known, it seems, in the NRA. Though it may not be clear to the total membership of NRA, this diversity of opinion his actually related more to choices of the best pathway to NRA's objectives than to any desire to change those objectives, or NRAs priorities. These objectives, contained on the first page of the NRA Bylaws, are to protect the right of the individual American citizen to keep and bear arms, to promote public safety, law and order, and the national defense, to train members of law enforcement agencies, the armed forces, the militia, and people of good repute in marksmanship, to foster and promote the shooting sports including competition and marksmanship, and to promote hunter safety and hunting as a shooting sport. I can assure you I know of no significant opinion in the councils of NRA to alter or to compromise these objectives. A major step was recently made in moderating factionalism, which, when conspicuous, is harmful to the operational effectiveness we all desire. President Keith M. Gaffaney recently called a special meeting of the leaders of the two most prominent factions in the NRA. A great step forward has beer made to establish unity. I am happy to publish, as follows, the report made to the Executive Committee on July 11, 1981 by the leaders of those groups: "On the evening of Friday July 10, 1981, an informal ad hoc group of representatives of those organizations known as the Federation for NRA and the Patriots for NRA gathered in Washington, D.C. for an interfactional conference. The purpose was to explore in good faith, the possibilities for cooperation and compromise between the groups for the greater good of NRA. Candid discussions of many problem areas ensued. Of the many proposals made, the members of the conference agreed to four steps designed to reduce the shrillness of the interfactional debate and to maintain the channels of communications opened by this conference. These steps are: (1)	A moratorium on bitterly partisan, campaign type letters to the Board of Directors. (2) A moratorium on fighting with each other in the outside press, especially including elements of the public media hostile to NRA. (3) An agreement to deal openly with all factions with regard to any potential petitioned proposals for amendments to NRA Bylaws at an Annual Members Meeting. Open dealing, in this context, includes prior notification and discussion of such proposals with an eye to finding possible areas of agreement between the factions. (4) A moratorium on advertisements promoting factional slates of candidates for the Board of Directors. It must be understood that the undersigned have so indicated their approval and support of these steps solely on their own parts and behalf, and that none of them has the power to control absolutely all segments of their own factions or any other, non-affiliated groups. However we have pledged individually to abide by this agreement personally and to exercise all possible influence wherever possible to that end. We believe this is to be a significant and beneficial move in the direction of greater harmony and efficiency within NRA. and request all Directors and other interested parties to join us in this effort. It is also understood of course, that the endorsement of these steps is not intended to be a formal binding agreement."
explanation: The text discusses efforts to reduce factionalism within the NRA and promote unity, but does not address gun regulation.

text: If the general public understood the truth about criminals and guns, there would be virtually no support for anything proposed by Sarah Brady or Bill Clinton or any of their allies in Congress. Gun control would be a non-issue. Crime and criminals are what the public is concerned about. You and I know the simple truth - that under existing federal laws, any violent convicted felons or drug dealers who pick up any firearm are committing serious federal crimes that would send them to prison for a long time. If only the laws were enforced. For the past several years, you and I have been demanding that the Clinton Administration carry out its sworn duty to uphold the federal laws. For the most part, the Administration has done virtually nothing to put armed criminals behind bars. Their answer is to "dissuade" violent criminals from buying guns from legal channels. The Brady law has been nothing more than a "catch and release" program. Al Gore has once again claimed the law has been used to turn away (and not arrest) 390,000 felons, drug dealers, stalkers and fugitives who walked into federally licensed gun dealers and committed mega federal felonies. That's the Brady law. Some brag. What good does it do to give lip service to "disarming" criminals when federal law enforcement almost never uses existing laws against criminals touching or using guns? I said almost never. There is a unique and shining exception. It is an effort conceived by a courageous group of federal prosecutors in Richmond, Virginia, who essentially bucked the Justice Department's standing policy of ignoring federal gun laws with respect to armed violent career criminals. This effort, endorsed and financially supported by the National Rifle Association, is called Project Exile. It involves total cooperation between local police and federal law enforcement, and between federal and state prosecutors. Project Exile puts into practice what we have been saying all along. Armed criminals are arrested and "exiled" from innocent citizens through absolute and certain federal prosecution and prison under existing laws. Criminals - drug dealers, felons, fugitives - all those categories that make the revolving-door statistics of the Brady law so obscene - are in deep trouble in Richmond if they possess any gun Punishment is swift and there is no escape for the guilty. And many innocent lives have been saved. Richmond is no longer among the top urban areas for homicide. In 1997, Richmond suffered the second highest per capita homicide rate in the nation. Violent crime - in the last six months - is down dramatically. Homicide is down 55 percent. The U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, whose office initiated Project Exile, told the Newport News Daily Press on January 23, 1998, that "officials were shocked ... at the extent of [Project Exile] suspects' criminal records. Several had between four and eight convictions for offenses as serious as robbery, abduction and murder." It is a fact that most violent crime in any community is committed by just a few repeat offenders. Criminal violence is a career - unlawful, mean and oftentimes deadly. The work of criminals always brings loss and pain to innocent victims. It undermines communities. In Richmond the work of federal prosecutors is removing many dangerous criminals from the streets. In Richmond, career opportunities for armed criminals are diminishing rapidly. Openings are going unfilled. The job market for the bad guys has slowed down - all due to Project Exile. Just this last year, local and federal officers put away 202 of Richmond's most dangerous violent offenders - mostly for illegally possessing guns. The average sentence was 56 months in a federal penitentiary. Additionally, there have been 259 related state arrests. That is considerably more federal prosecutions than have been made nationwide under the entire enforcement history of the Brady law since 1993. Unlike drug dealers in other cities, Richmond dope peddlers are beginning to go unarmed, according to local police. They know the law. They know the risk. And the risk isn't Sarah Brady's vision of "disarmament." In Richmond - thanks to Project Exile - criminals know and understand the risk of possessing and using firearms. For the peaceable people of Richmond and the surrounding areas, Project Exile is no secret at all. The message is broadcast on television, radio and is placarded on busses. Armed criminals will get federal jail time. Yet for the rest of the country, this success is still under wraps. Don't expect anybody in the executive branch of government in Washington, D.C., to talk about it. Handgun Control, Inc., and its political clones in government do not want the average non-gun owning American to know what every NRA member knows - that it is already as illegal as it can be for criminals to possess firearms. All of the very tough laws covering possession of firearms by felons and drug dealers were made even more stringent during our fight to enact the Firearms Owners Protection Act in 1986. Sarah Brady and Handgun Control. Inc., opposed those tough criminal sanctions. Sarah Brady - just before the big push to enact the Brady Bill in 1993, said, "I think people around the country are shocked when they realize that we don't have federal laws when it comes to guns ... ." That was a lie. But after all the years of the Brady law, it is a lie that seems to be true in practice today. If the criminal laws are not enforced - or even recognized by this lawless Clinton Administration - the public might just believe that there are no laws to be enforced. Project Exile is proving otherwise, and you must see that it is given the spotlight of truth it deserves.
explanation: The text discusses Project Exile, a program to prosecute armed criminals, and critiques the lack of enforcement of existing gun laws, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: If you think PETA is just a benign bunch of animal lovers, this column is a must-read for you. PETA, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals, is the largest, wealthiest and most high-profile group of animal "rights" extremists in the world. And it is linked to a growing network of embedded cells of dangerous people willing to achieve their ends through violence. If you look past all the puppies, propaganda and PR stunts, PETA's agenda won't improve animal welfare, but abolish it. If PETA has its way, there will be no hunting and therefore no wildlife conservation, no wetlands protection or habitat development. The subsequent disease, mass starvation and die-off of animals are unthinkable. And that's just the tip of the iceberg that should sink their titanic lunacy. Nobody invests more money in wildlife conservation than hunters. Yet we are the targets of these extremists, despite our unwavering commitment to land for wildlife research, habitat conservation, species protection and game law enforcement. In contrast, PETA's so-called "animal shelters" have become killing fields for dogs and cats. At its Norfolk, Va., headquarters, PETA has reportedly killed more than 10,000 dogs and cats since 1998. Yet many Americans don't know that PETA wants much more than to take a fishing pole from every child's hand, ban milk from their breakfasts and shut down all their circuses, zoos and aquariums. PETA wants much more than to take away seeing-eye dogs from the blind and to take away bomb-sniffing dogs from our airports. PETA wants to stop medical advancements that use animal research in any way. That would eliminate almost every major medical achievement in the 20th century. If PETA has its way, there will be no treatment for diabetes, heart disease, infection or chronic pain. There will be no vaccines, chemotherapy, organ transplants or bypass surgery. And if PETA has its way, there may never be a cure for AIDS, Alzheimer's, cancer, cystic fibrosis, multiple sclerosis or any other human suffering. This isn't theoretical stuff. These radicals have the money and spare time to devise ways to stop the world's miracle workers. That's how PETA's agenda against hunting is consistent with its agenda against medicine. The consequence of PETA's agenda would be staggering: no less than a die-off of human beings comparable to the aftermath of a thermo-nuclear war or a devastating asteroid strike. What's more, PETA's agenda is being forced upon society with acts of violence and terrorism. PETA has contributed to movements like the Earth Liberation Front (ELF) and the Animal Liberation Front (ALF), which have committed a thousand firebomb attacks and caused more than $110 million in property damage. This eco-terrorism movement is so dangerous, the FBI has declared it America's No. 1 domestic terrorist threat. They've upstaged al Qaeda as the greatest terrorist threat on American soil. Scientists, doctors and their families are having property destroyed and are getting hate mail, letters loaded with razor blades and rat poison, and death threats and bomb threats. The tragedy is that it's working. Medical research didn't budget for security against extremists. Our most promising labs are being shut down. Studies on the verge of medical breakthrough are screeching to a halt. We're losing some of our best minds to their madness. That madness is being packaged and pitched to our kids, too. One of PETA's handouts at elementary schools shows a wild-eyed mommy in her bloody apron hacking away at a live rabbit with a butcher knife. The headline reads: "YOUR MOMMY KILLS ANIMALS." Another PETA comic book called A Rat's Life encourages kids to pet rats. Its kids' website teaches kids how to be an "animal rights rebel," how to ridicule kids who drink milk and how to boycott classes. Animal "rights" extremism is a belief system based on 100 percent emotion and zero science, riddled with hypocrisy and roiling with contempt for humans. They're so consumed by self-righteousness that they rationalize intimidation, property destruction, assault, arson and bombing to meet their ends. We must expose these animal "rights" extremists and fight their dogma with the same strength and commitment we deploy to protecting the Second Amendment or we risk losing our hunting heritage for generations to come.
explanation: The text discusses the dangers of PETA and animal rights extremism, but does not address gun regulation.

text: SINCE the days when the backwoods gunsmith turned out Kentucky Rifles by hand, the arms and ammunition industry in this country has been an intensely individualistic business. Even though some of the organizations had passed beyond the stage of one-man control, and into large corporate structures before the turn of the century, they nevertheless retained from the management standpoint the individualist attitude. Epidemics of price cutting ravaged the industry periodically. In an effort to "get the jump on the other fellow," a manufacturer would bring out new guns and new cartridges without any reference to the actual need for guns or cartridges of that particular type. Not desiring to be outdone, other companies would then advertise guns and ammunition of a somewhat similar type, but with presumably different features. The net result has been the creation of such a complexity of arms, cartridges and loads that no company can produce enough arms or cartridges of any one type to be able to take advantage of its production facilities to bring down the price of arms and ammunition to the consumer. The standardization and simplification which alone have made possible the continued reduction in the price of automobiles and practically all other manufactured articles, has been non-existent in the arms and ammunition industry. The production on some guns and most cartridges has been so limited as to make it almost a custom proposition. Shooters have suffered from the resultant high costs, and because shooters would not or could not buy as much as they wanted at the prevailing high prices, the industry in turn has suffered. The Government of the United States, now bending anxious efforts to the revitalization of industry, is itself in part to blame for the existing condition. The arms and ammunition manufacturers built tremendous plants for the production of war-time munitions. The plants were built at the peak of construction costs, and notes and bonds issued to help pay for them. At the end of the war the Government cancelled contracts with utter disregard for the financial obligations of the companies, and since the war practically no Government business has been given to the private plants. The interest on the notes and bonds had to be met, and taxes had to be paid. All of which did its part to keep the cost of shooting equipment up, at a time when prices should have been drastically adjusted downward. Receiverships were the inevitable result; and out of them, within the past few months, have emerged new set-ups which give promise of a brighter future for both the arms and ammunition industry and the sportsmen of the country. Much of the dead wood of over-capitalization has perforce been cut away in the working out of mergers, the perfection of which must inevitably eliminate a considerable amount of the intense individualism which heretofore has been a millstone around the neck of the industry, and has in the long run resulted only in higher prices to the consumer. Enough of the individualism remains, however, to eliminate any fear of the development of a monopoly for the purpose of maintaining unreasonable prices, even as the type of the companies and individuals involved in the mergers eliminates any such probability. It now remains to be seen whether or not the dominant groups will take advantage of the opportunity which is presented for the first time in the history of American gun and ammunition building, to cut away the rest of the dead wood which is propping up the price structure - dead wood consisting of an utterly useless and economically - indefensible variety of gun models, cartridge types and cartridge loads. It is difficult to picture the situation that would exist in the automobile industry if in addition to the 1933 models there were also being offered to the public 1932 models, 1931 models, and all the other models back to 1908, simply because certain purchasers of those particular models liked them and would buy them again if they were still available. Impossible as such a situation may appear, it is nevertheless exactly the condition that has been allowed to develop in the arms and ammunition business. There must be progress. New guns, new actions, new cartridges, and new loads must be developed. And when a better load for a particular cartridge is developed, then by all the rules of efficient manufacture, the old and less satisfactory load should be discontinued. To continue it means a reduced volume of sale for both loads, increased manufacturing cost, increased distributing cost, increased advertising cost, and the raising of legitimate doubt in the mind of the purchaser as to whether the new cartridge is really superior to the old. The arms and ammunition industry under the old scheme of things has been in the impossible position of trying to move forward and stand still at the same time. The inevitable result has been that it has gone backward. The American shooting public will watch with keen and intelligent interest to see whether the unquestioned ability which has been assembled in the perfection of these recent mergers is backed by the courage to embark upon an economically sound manufacturing and merchandising program; a program which will mean increased profits to the industry even - while it means decreased prices to the consumer - a program which, while drawing fully upon the experience of the past, can nevertheless discard the products of the past and build products for the future. A program, indeed, in which the essential element is the courage to say, "Sorry, but we have discontinued that, because we know this is better."
explanation: The text discusses the history and challenges of the arms and ammunition industry, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Today I'm asking you to help me on behalf of NRA and every law-abiding gun owner in this nation. In dozens of interviews, I've tried to set the record straight. But anti-gun members of the media parrot the lies of gun control groups and continue to maling NRA by lying about our positions and strength. They ignore a crashed criminal justice system that is no longer working and push the same tired gun bans that affect only honest American citizens. They try to make NRA, instead of crime, the issue. Let me give you just a few examples of the absurd comments that are continually made. NRA opposes restrictions on "cop-killer bullets." The truth is, NRA wrote and fully supported passage of the existing law which bans the sale of so-called cop-killer bullets to anyone other than the military and law enforcement. It also protects commonly used hunting and other ammunition that would have been banned if the original bill had been passed. Semi-automatic "assault rifles" are the weapons of choice of criminals. Only machine guns are, by definition, assault rifles. The semi-auto, military-style firearms the media calls assault rifle are functionally the same as all the other 30 million lawfully owned self-loading firearms in the nation and are actually used in about 0.5% of all the homicides occurring in this country. The Second Amendment provides for the militia, like the National Guard, and has nothing to do with individual rights. As recently as 1990 the Supreme Court ruled that "people" - a word "employed in select parts of the Constitution," specifically the Preamble, First, Second, Fourth, Ninth and Tenth Amendments, means the same thing throughout - the rights of the individual. NRA has lost the support of gun owners. NRA is now in the longest sustained growth in its history with over three million members. In the past 18 months, we have added over 600,000 net new members, more than the combined	memberships of all the gun control groups in the U.S. This is just a sample of the lies perpetuated by certain powerful members of the media in an attempt to "put away NRA." It won't happen. When you face such lies, call NRA Research & Information for the straight answer then confront our opponents with the truth. Join me in the fight. Together we can prove, once and for all - it's not the guns - it's the criminals.
explanation: The text discusses media misrepresentations of the NRA's positions and the need to counter anti-gun propaganda, directly addressing gun regulation.

text: Once each year, during the month of August, a portion of the southern shore of Lake Erie becomes the campus for thousands of American citizens who attend special courses of instruction in rifle and pistol marksmanship. The schools are sponsored by the National Board for the Promotion of Rifle Practice and the National Rifle Association of America to develop qualified instructors who will train our citizens in the use of the basic military weapons of national defense. All of our great wars have been fought in the main by citizen armies. An essential element of preparedness is training our people to use the weapons which will be handed to them upon mobilization. The advent of the nuclear-missile age has not dispensed with the soldier's personal arm, but merely complemented it with new elements of military force. The very nature of the new weapons of war enhance rather than diminish the value of the personal weapon. More than ever before, the individual soldier and the individual civilian will be forced in time of war to rely upon the weapon in his hands and on his own ability to use it effectively if he is to survive. The mission of the Small Arms Firing Schools at Camp Perry is to bring to civilians and to members of the various components of the Armed Forces, not reached through training programs conducted within the active military services, information concerning the most modem methods of marksmanship instruction in order to raise the standards of performance in the use of individual military arms by the citizens of our country. Each school consists of a basic class and an advanced class. These two courses are designed to standardize the instruction received by military, reserve, and civilian personnel. Students in the basic class are taught the techniques required to form good shooting habits. In the advanced class, emphasis is placed on the role of the student as a coach and an instructor. Students attending the rifle school fire the M1 rifle and those attending the pistol school fire the .45 caliber pistol. Instructors are selected individuals from the United States Army Infantry School at Fort Benning, Georgia. The purpose of the Police Pistol School at Camp Perry is to present specialized up-to-date techniques of law enforcement tactics involving the use of firearms. The school affords law enforcement personnel an opportunity to discuss methods of training and to fire pistol training courses. It provides an opportunity for police agencies to send representatives who will be qualified, upon successful completion of the course, to establish or improve law enforcement training programs in local communities. Instructors are selected from the Armed Forces, the Border Patrol, and police departments for their outstanding ability in a particular phase of police instruction. They are changed each year to provide different views on training and methods used. The Junior and Tyro School at Camp Perry is conducted for novice shooters. Instruction includes basic fundamentals of marksmanship and match firing with .22 caliber rifles. The objective of this school and the evening classes in Leadership instruction is to develop and test new techniques and training aids for teaching marksmanship. Instructors are selected individual NRA members who serve without compensation. The significance of the Camp Perry Marksmanship Schools to shooters is indicated by the fact that attendance for 1958 exceeded 4,000. Their value to our country will be reflected as these qualified people return to their military units and civilian organizations to teach marksmanship to others. A prepared citizenry, trained to do a soldier's job with a soldier's skill when necessity calls, is essential to a strong America. Marksmanship training in time of peace is vital to preparedness in case of war.
explanation: The text describes the Small Arms Firing Schools at Camp Perry and their role in marksmanship training, but does not address gun regulation.

text: With Bill Clinton as a lame duck President with nothing to lose, firearms owners will be targeted by a host of truly evil proposals by his Department of Justice (DOJ). The major thrust of this attack - covered by nearly 50 individual "initiatives" - is new, couched in terms of "gun safety," "victims' rights" "racketeering," "juvenile crime," "consumer safety," "medical societal costs" and "firearms injury." That's just the beginning. False language has become a well-honed weapon. Nothing is what it seems. If a combination of these proposals becomes law, people who are now peaceable and innocent gun owners surely could become victims of a kind of political purge not seen before in America. The DOJ's working list - obtained from an unimpeachable source inside the department - included "initiatives" designed to so overwhelm individual firearms owners with criminal and related civil actions that they would be financially paralyzed and could not possibly defend themselves against legions of government lawyers. It's real. Let me tell you about the worst of it - those "initiatives" that are designed to savage individual gun owners under new criminal and civil sanctions. And the best way is to paint a hypothetical example. It is someone you and I know. A nice person. A decent man targeted sometime in the future, if the Clinton proposals become law. Note that the words in bold type are quotes from actual DOJ thumbnail descriptions of what's coming. In this case, the victim is a middle-aged family man who lives in rural southern Indiana, very close to the Illinois border. He is a collector, who started his hobby as a youngster. He owns more than 30 firearms. It is a collection that he has improved over the years with wise trades and buying and selling firearms - regularly upgrading. We all know this man. He's not a criminal. His only connection with street crime is the same as yours or mine - he's worried about violence in America. This man lives on a farm that has been in his family for generations, and he hopes it will go to his children someday. His father, a widower, lives not far away, in town, just across the border in Illinois. His Dad is also a collector and keeps a few guns in his little retirement apartment. Let's call our friend Bob. One of the mandates of the Clinton law is to "Require owners of firearms 'arsenals' to provide notice to law enforcement." Bob doesn't consider his collection an "arsenal." He doesn't think the requirement applies to him. He thinks his property is his business. So he doesn't report it. That's a crime. In the course of improving his gun collection, Bob bought five guns last year from his local federally-licensed dealers. He has signed the new BATF Form 4473, swearing to the statement "I further understand that my repetitive purchase of firearms for purpose of resale or profit without a Federal Firearms License is a violation of law," (for more on this, see this month's "ILA Report"). Oh, yes. This past Christmas, he gave his Dad a crispy Parker DH 20-ga., something his father always dreamed of. It was a straight gift. After all, his Dad lives just 12 miles away. Technically, under GCA '68, it is a crime though unintentionally committed. It's a crime only because the government says it is, not because it is an act that is intrinsically wrong or hurtful. Bob's act is unwitting and he has no criminal intent. His father has no criminal intent or knowledge. No matter. Then some real criminals break into Bob's home and take two handguns. (The rest of Bob's guns - all insured - are hidden in the walls of his house.) The bad guys - with long violent felony records - travel to Evansville, Indiana, where they kill a clerk in a large discount store. The men are caught with the two guns - purchased from dealers - are traced back to Bob. Because the Clinton law contains a section to "Extend federal jurisdiction to all murders committed with a firearm," the killing of the store clerk is taken out of the hands of local Evansville detectives and becomes an FBI case. In the course of investigating the murder, and the theft, a joint FBI/BATF task force descends on Bob. They have all the 4473s Bob has signed over the years, and they have search warrants for all of those guns and any unknown guns in his unreported "arsenal." Bob is charged with failing to report his "arsenal," with 27 counts of dealing without a license, covering all the guns he legally bought and sold over the years which were legally covered by 4473s. Federal agents, of course, have the serial numbers and descriptions of all of Bob's guns after getting them from his insurance company, since to obtain insurance Bob had to comply with Clinton law provisions to "Require gun owners to record the make, model and serial number of their firearms as a condition of obtaining gun insurance...." In the process of searching Bob's own records, they find that he has given his Dad the shotgun. They charge Bob with transferring a gun to an out-of-state resident. A felony. They tell the media he is an "interstate gun-runner." Under the Clinton crime law section to "Authorize the criminal forfeiture of firearms used in the commission of any federal crime, including authorization to destroy such firearms upon forfeiture," federal prosecutors file a forfeiture action against Bob's guns. It's called United States v. 33 Firearms. In order to oppose the forfeiture, Bob has to post a bond of 10% of the collection's worth - not his figure, the government's, which the prosecutors call the "street value." For Bob, it's a lot of money - just for the privilege of fighting the government. Bob's Dad is also charged with the felony of having received the Christmas gun. The old gentleman is also arrested for another felony under the Clinton law's amendments to "the drug free school zone statute ... to expand the list of protected areas to include pre-schools, nursery schools, and day care centers." His retirement home is within 1,000 ft. of a day care center, so it's illegal for him to have his guns in his own home. But there's more in store for Bob's Dad. In the course of investigating the father, the BATF discovers that in 1944 - during his WWII Navy service - while on shore leave, sailors from his ship had gotten into a scuffle with some drunken dock workers. It was self-defense, but Bob's Dad pleaded guilty to simple assault. Under the Clinton law, there are provisions to "Establish firearms disability for misdemeanor crimes of violence." That means that the misdemeanor conviction from 1944 puts the old veteran in the same category as convicted violent felons. He is a prohibited person, and it's a felony for him to even touch a gun. I almost forgot. Bob talked to his wife about getting Dad his Christmas shotgun - so there is a conspiracy, and she is charged with felony conspiracy under Clinton law provisions "to provide that a conspiracy to commit a firearms offense shall be punishable to the same maximum term as for the underlying substantive offense. So much for Bob's family. But there is more in store for poor Bob. Much more. The federal government has just begun.  The Clinton law includes sections to  "Amend the RICO statute to ad certain federal offenses involving the illegal transfer of firearms to the list of RICO predicates ... and facilitate the prosecution of certain RICO cases by providing the prosecutors need not prove that a defendant personally agreed to commit any acts of racketeering." What that means for Bob is that he is now charged with being a "racketeer" under the Racketeer Influenced And Corrupt Organizations Act. Bob is now lumped in the same category as mobsters, international money launderers, drug kingpins and murder-for-hire killers. This law is the nuclear strike of federal criminal statutes. Under RICO, the government prosecutors "freeze" some of Bob's assets - those they can broadly claim to connect to Bob's trading in guns over the years, as "racketeering." Remember, he's only been charged with a crime, not convicted. In the meantime, Bob is hit with a civil suit encouraged under a provision of the Clinton law to "Establish private cause of action for persons injured by firearms which were not stored safely." In this case, the two handguns stolen by Bob's burglars. This suit is filed by the family of the Evansville store clerk murdered by the burglars. The civil legal action is encouraged by lawyers representing an anti-gun group which gets federal grant funding under Clinton law provisions to "Raise the federal firearms and/or ammunition tax to support prevention, safety, victim, or medical initiatives targeting gun violence." In addition, U.S. Justice Department lawyers - from the Civil Division, this time - enter the suit with their own briefs against Bob. Their part of the suit has us do with restitution under "victims' rights" sections in the Clinton law "to restrain defendant's assets pending trial and sentencing when it reasonably appears those assets may be dissipated...." So they move civilly to freeze all of Bob's assets. Now, he can't use his bank account. Or credit cards. Can't pay his bills. He can't mortgage the farm to get a lawyer. He can't sell any personal property to pay for a defense. He can't even get a loan. Yet the federal government has unlimited resources - Bob's and our tax dollars. Oh, yes, the family of the murdered clerk isn't the only plaintiff who files against Bob. Under the Clinton law, for the purposes of victim restitution, "Witnesses to violent crime are by definition 'victims' for purposes of any Federal statute or state program using Federal funds designated for victims." There were more than 30 people in that big Evansville discount store who now claim to be witnesses and are thus "victims" entitled to restitution. It's a nightmare. It's unwinnable. The power that would be used against individual peaceable gun owners is designed to be literally overwhelming. How does Bob fight any of this? His assets are frozen; the criminal charges against him are impossible; his guns are gone; his family is wrecked. He can't afford a lawyer. Bob doesn't fight. He rolls over, prior to the point the government rolls over him. How would you fight it? You could not. Not even if you were rich as a king. There is more - at least 30 other proposals I could tell you about, just as bad as those that be used against our fictional friend. In all of them, we - you and I - are the target, not violent street criminals. But thank goodness these are merely proposals - draft legislation that will have to clear the Second Amendment majority you elected to Congress. Can this really happen? Yes. It can if we fail to fight. We fight by keeping the NRA strong and united. By not brooking any divisive bickering that would destroy our ability to remain a powerful force in mainstream American politics. The bottom line is, we are facing the most clever and ruthless enemy ever. How do we fight? We fight by understanding the meaning of words and phrases and the ultimate consequences of these proposals. We fight by passing on that knowledge to our friends and neighbors. If "victim compensation" really means horrible "gun control," don't be fooled. When they surface as legislation, these proposals will mean what the actual legal language says, no matter how they are cloaked by lofty descriptions. You fight by using your voices, by writing Congress. I will let you know when these proposals surface, and when and how you must respond. You fight by defeating these proposals to keep them from becoming the law of the land. We still are the most powerful grassroots lobby in the nation but only if we believe and respond, only if we keep democracy working. And we can do that only if we remain a cohesive, disciplined, ordered and centered organization.
explanation: The text is a tribute to Ammon B. Critchfield and the history of Camp Perry, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Deeply rooted in American tradition is the desire of a youngster to have a gun of his own. The history of our fight for independence; the many legends that grew up as the frontiers of the West were rolled back; indeed, much of our more popular literature, movies, radio, and television; all combine to keep alive the part played in America by strong men with the ability to shoot straight. Small wonder that at Christmas one of the most enchanting of all gifts continues to be that longed-for 'gun of his own'. With it goes from father to son a great wealth of American tradition, all wrapped up in the process of a youngster becoming a man. Guns have been and can continue to be constructive tools, used to build healthy minds and bodies, to develop self-discipline, initiative, and team spirit in order to mold the youth of America into better citizens and better sportsmen. Hunting and shooting are wholesome forms of recreation which may, in safety, be employed for a lifetime. Why, then, are we so often admonished in press and radio and television, "Don't give a boy a gun for Christmas!"? Why this sentiment on the part of some people that guns, in spite of our hallowed history and tradition, are somehow evil things from which our youth must be sheltered and protected? The answer, of course, is in our changing environment. Our traditions live along with us but our way of life changes. Years ago it was necessary and accepted that every youngster be intimately acquainted with firearms. He learned to use and appreciate a gun as a tool of everyday life. A father considered a boy's education with a gun as much a part of his upbringing as the three R's. Today, too many fathers make the mistake of giving the gun only without the priceless ingredient of knowledge and skill to use the gun safely and well. Some fathers feel that they are not sufficiently experienced to teach their children. Fortunately, no child need be deprived of an opportunity to learn safety and skill with firearms because his parents do not happen to be expert shooters. There are many others who are able and willing to do the job with help and support. The National Rifle Association of America, with its 300,000 individual members and 8,000 affiliated local groups, has proved beyond question that shooting can be the safest of sports. Millions of boys and girls all over America have learned to shoot and earned awards in its Junior program since schoolboy rifle practice was begun in 1907. Through the efforts of 25,000 volunteer instructors in its Hunter Safety Training Course, the NRA has taught proper gun handling to more than 500,000 young people since 1949. Schools, summer camps, scout troops, and clubs, plus veteran, fraternal, and patriotic organizations have joined forces to make safe shooting available to any youngster and his parents. Don't give ear to the prophets of doom who preach "Don't give a gun for Christmas!" The ownership and proper use of a gun is forever bound up in our American heritage. It is as natural for an American youngster to want a gun as it is natural for him to want to grow up a free man. At the same time give heed to your own responsibility - a responsibility which was exercised by your forefathers as a matter of course. When you give your child a gun, give him also the knowledge, the skill, and the sense of responsibility which is a part of being a shooter, so that he may appreciate his gun and use it safely and in complete enjoyment all his life. This year, let's see to it that our young people get more than a gun for Christmas!
explanation: The text discusses the tradition of giving guns as gifts to youngsters and the importance of firearms safety education, but does not address gun regulation.

text: There was a familiar objection to the National Matches in the fifteen years prior to Pearl Harbor. It was that the tryouts for the Service Teams and subsequent participation in "tune-up" programs and "the Nationals" took officers away from their own organizations "just when they are most needed." Some regimental and division commanders would use every means at their disposal to get rid of an officer who wanted to participate in the National Matches as a match official or member of a Service Team squad. The error and narrowness of such a viewpoint are now demonstrated in the trials of actual warfare (as the error of numerous other peacetime objections to the National Match idea has also been demonstrated). Writing in the Command and General Staff School's "Military Review" (April, 1944), Lieutenant Colonel Jay C. Whitehair in an article titled "Introduction to a Task Force" says - "An officer may expect to be placed on a task force staff with officers whom he has never met before...(Task forces are constantly altered dependent on their mission.) "This means that there is not the background of close association which one may expect in a more permanent organization, as, for example, a division staff, and brings out the need of an officer being prepared to start functioning immediately with officers with perhaps entirely different backgrounds than his own. Needless to say, the ability to meet people and size them up is of paramount importance and the necessity for a friendly attitude is no less important than on any other staff. It is also definitely worth while checking, by whatever means available, into the background of any officers who have special functions with the staff." Aside from maneuvers employing task forces, there is probably no activity sponsored by the Armed Services in peacetime which affords as good an opportunity for the officers of all branches to learn the personalities, habits, strong points, and weaknesses under pressure of the officers in sister Services as is provided by the weeks of training and competition culminating in the National Team Match. Soldiers, sailors, marines, national guardsmen and reservists, men from many divisions, posts, and stations, brought together by a common interest in shooting, are forced by circumstances at the National Matches and preceding events to learn to adjust themselves to one another, to size up their teammates and their opponents. Solid, enduring friendships are formed which jump all boundaries of Branch and Service. How many precious hours of getting acquainted, of sizing up the other man, would be saved in mobilizing a Task Force Staff if the men on that staff were all Men of Perry! Even among the best friends of the National Matches and the NRA competitive program, there has been too little realization of the true breadth of the constructive values attending these annual events. In this war, as in previous ones, we are relearning forgotten lessons-relearning them, unfortunately, the hard way!
explanation: The text discusses the value of the National Matches in fostering camaraderie and training among military officers, but does not address gun regulation.

text: THE announcement that the Hercules Powder Company is discontinuing the sale of smokeless rifle powders in canisters, and the concurrent report that duPont, while continuing canister sales, will, like Hercules, discontinue canister labels carrying suggested charges, comes as a distinct disappointment to a large section of the rifle and pistol-shooting public. While it is true that only a small percentage of our shooters are reloaders, it is also true that in many communities those men who are sufficiently interested in the game to "roll their own" are the spark-plugs who keep the wheels turning in their local clubs. They are frequently the men whose keen interest places them in the forefront of the voters who actively combat anti-firearms legislation. They are the men who most consistently and enthusiastically talk guns and shooting to all who will listen. They are the men who first bring new guns and new gadgets into the neighborhood, and thereby serve as missionaries for the arms and ammunition companies. In many cases they are men who could not shoot enough to maintain their interest unless they could reload. In many other cases they are men who can afford memberships in expensive golf and yacht clubs, but who stay in the shooting game because they like to work with their heads and their hands at some hobby. Deprived of the opportunity to reload, they will turn to model-building or radio - and another valuable booster will be lost to the shooting game. There are thousands of police officers who are receiving training and gradually becoming enthusiastic shooters, whose departments could not secure the funds to carry on if reloading were not possible. There are hundreds of other police departments just becoming interested, who will revert to their old status of pistol ignorance and anti-gun propaganda if they are informed that reloading is either difficult or necessarily dangerous. Just why is this policy announced at a time when the rifle and pistol game seemed destined to reach new highs in popularity? "Because", say the powder companies, "we are afraid some one will blow up his gun and we will be sued for damages. We are not trying to force the discontinuance of reloading: we are merely leaving it up to the manufacturers of the bullets, cases, and primers which the reloader uses, to recommend powder charges. Because of the rapid changes which have been and are being made in components, each lot of powder we make has to be tested with the exact components it is to be loaded with, or excessive pressures may result-and then we might be sued for damages. We have always lost money on canister business anyhow, and one damage suit would wipe out a large part of our profits on all the rifle and pistol powder we sell". What of the manufacturers of components? Will they take the place of the powder companies in recommending charges? That remains to be seen. None wants to take the responsibility for such recommendations unless their own components are used, both shell and primer. Their gross business on components is so small that a damage suit would wipe out a year's profits. So the matter rests. The Institute of Sporting Arms and Ammunition Manufacturers has long had a Committee on Standardization. It is a good committee, and has done good work in some fields. But this Committee seems impotent to produce any results which will bring order out of chaos in the present situation, and return the reloader to his loading bench. The National Rifle Association definitely believes that reloading, sensibly done, is an important part and an integral part of rifle and pistol-shooting promotion in this country. The present situation is going to do no one any good. If permitted to long continue, it will do definite harm.
explanation: The text discusses the discontinuation of smokeless powder sales by Hercules and duPont and its impact on reloaders, but does not address gun regulation.

text: Shall we, or shall we not, have universal military service in the United States of America? This is a question which should be decided in 1945. Nothing is to be gained by waiting for that indefinite time vaguely referred to as "after the war." The time to decide a momentous question is the instant all pertinent facts are available, the evidence fresh, and the reasons clearly defined in the minds of those who must give the evidence and those who must decide the issue. Certainly all the pertinent facts are available now. Certainly those best equipped to present the evidence are available in greater force now than they will ever be again. Certainly the reasons impelling the discussion and demanding a decision are clearer now than they will be when the fog is rising from innumerable peacetime political conflicts within and without our borders. Why, then, delay the discussion and the decision? There are two reasons. First, the groups who oppose universal sendee know that their one best hope of killing such a law is to delay its consideration until the witnesses are scattered and gone and the need forgotten in the easygoing fashion of America-between-wars. So the opponents talk about "further research" and "coolheaded deliberation," knowing full well that the political coward, seeking to straddle an issue he fears, will always vote to appoint a committee in preference to voting "yea" or "nay" where his position can be seen by all his constituents. Thus the second reason, political cowardice, stems from the first. Because popular opinion in America does, at this time, definitely favor a permanent universal service law, the political straddlers would vote "yea" if forced now to vote. Delay the whole thing until the bungling, lost time, and useless casualties of this war have been forgotten, until the, soft psychology of America-is-between-wars has again taken control of our mass thinking, and the few opponents of universal service plus the political straddlers will once more leave an unprepared America standing on the auction block before the international pirates and brigands of the next generation. It is true that the technical details involved in drafting the best kind of universal service law call for patient study and intelligent compromise by the best available military, naval, and civilian minds. The strength, length of service, type of training, order of call into service for regular, national guard, and reserve units; the method of selection, training, and promotion of officers and noncommissioned officers; the question of exemptions and what to do with those exempted, are matters of utmost importance. Full hearings should be extended to the men who are now too busy fighting this war to take time out to talk about fighting the next one. It would be a political error and against the best interests of the national defense to attempt to enact in 1945 a revised National Defense Act incorporating a complete plan for universal military service. The details must wait until men now fighting under the handicap imposed by our catch-as-catch-can "defense" policy can sit around the conference table with business men. educators, and congressmen and work out a sensible, workable. American-type plan. However, these very men, who must fill in the details, know from bitter experience that if the principle of universal service is to be written into American law it must be done before this war ends. This is the cold, hard core of the matter. The badly assorted and not-too-logical opponents of universal service realize the fact and intend to capitalize on it by seeking delay. The proponents of the principle of universal service are not, themselves, too well coordinated on the details but they can combine their efforts on a drive to secure the enactment of a law establishing the principle that every man who lives under the shelter of the American flag has the definite duty to prepare himself to efficiently defend that Flag and the principles it represents. Those who sincerely want that principle written into law will waste no time in pressing their views before the new Congress. Let the details wait.
explanation: The text discusses the debate over universal military service and its importance for national defense, but does not address gun regulation.

text: During recent months, millions of firearms owners, settling back to watch some of their favorite television shows, have been snapped to attention by the blatant anti-gun sermonizing marring the plots of several crime dramas. Shows including MacGyver, The Equalizer and even a daytime TV soap opera, have intentionally, and as lawyers say, "with malicious aforethought," taken up the anti-gun cause. Plots center around themes that seem to spring straight from the pen of Sarah Brady, while leading characters deliver callously scripted lines that denounce and degrade our Second Amendment rights. These thinly veiled editorial attacks hide their message under the all-encompassing umbrella of entertainment  - alleged fiction, if you will. But the facts are this: the episodes offer prime time commentary that is little more than commercial advertising worth millions of dollars. Pro-gun advocates are not allowed to respond nor are they offered equal time. These emotional anti-gun tirades are designed to influence millions of impressionable minds. And I, for one, am sick and tired of such underhanded dealing. Unfortunately we at the NRA have no direct control over TV scripts and the political attitudes of scriptwriters. But we owe it to our cause to rise up in protest against what are some of the most slippery tactics our enemies have yet stooped to employ. A deluge of letters and calls directed to television networks that air anti-gun segments will draw immediate attention. After all, America's 70 million firearms owners have tremendous economic clout. We are the people whom television advertisers are attempting to reach. Let's strike out by utilizing the power of the free enterprise system. If we do this, rest assured that we'll get our message across. If you view a television program that contains anti-gun propaganda, immediately call the local network affiliate that aired the program and protest. Better yet - and to be really effective - call and write the parent network and lodge a clear, concise complaint. Be sure to mention the name of the program and when and where the offensive episode aired. The addresses and telephone numbers of the major networks are listed below. Sponsors of anti-gun programming must also be made aware of our displeasure. This is more difficult to accomplish. Due to the complicated nature of purchasing air time, companies rarely know the exact content of programs that eventually carry their commercial messages. That's why the NRA wants you to let us help. If you're offended by an anti-gun message appearing on your local TV programming, quickly note the name of the show plus the time, place, date, local network affiliate and the names of firms providing commercial sponsorship. Send this information to the NRA's Public Education Division, 1600 Rhode Island Ave, NW, Washington, D.C. 20036. And please - be sure to tell us exactly what you saw. If possible, video tape the show and send it along as evidence. We'll return all tapes. Armed with your input and alerted by your eyes and ears, the NRA can notify sponors who have unwittingly paid for anti-gun programming. This task has become more complex now that anti-gun factions have invaded the entire entertainment industry. A blatant anti-firearms editorial, cleverly concealed within its dramatic script, is difficult to intercept before the damage is done. Yet, with your help, we at the NRA will continue to monitor this situation to bring this travesty under control. Believe me, 70 million outraged gun owners can exert some prime-time pressure.
